A useful counterweight to the Memoirs: it helps distinguish the minister as he was from the figure he wished posterity to remember.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: Witte
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: S. V. Ilyin
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: A popular biography in the Lives of Remarkable People series, lighter than the academic studies.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: A biography of Witte published by Molodaya Gvardiya in the Lives of Remarkable People series. The channel recommends it as a more accessible alternative to Ananyich and Ganelin’s scholarly biography. For readers who want a continuous account of his life after the posts on “Count Half-Sakhalin”, without a full scholarly apparatus.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: Russia and International Capital, 1897–1914
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: Boris Ananyich
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: Loans, the gold ruble and dependence on French money: a good companion to Molodyakov.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: A study of the money behind Witte’s empire: foreign loans, the gold ruble and growing dependence on French capital. The channel recommends it alongside Molodyakov’s book on the Franco-Russian alliance. Where that explains why St Petersburg and Paris drew together, this shows what the alliance cost in rubles and francs. It matters to Dalny and Port Arthur because French money reached the Chinese Eastern Railway and Kwantung through the Russo-Chinese Bank.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: S. Yu. Witte: Financier, Politician, Diplomat
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: A. P. Korelin, S. A. Stepanov
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: On the channel’s short list for readers who want to learn more about Witte.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: A book from the further-reading list accompanying the Witte series. Its title names three sides of his career: finance, politics and diplomacy. The channel covers the same subjects through the gold ruble, the October Manifesto, the agreement with Li Hongzhang and the Treaty of Portsmouth. The channel’s author has not offered a separate assessment of this book.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: S. Yu. Witte as a Diplomat
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: A. V. Ignatyev
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: On the channel’s short list for readers chiefly interested in Witte’s diplomacy.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: A further-reading recommendation on Witte’s foreign policy. For the channel’s readers, its relevance is above all the Far East: the treaty with Li Hongzhang, the Chinese Eastern Railway, the Kwantung lease and the Portsmouth negotiations that earned Witte the nickname “Count Half-Sakhalin”. The channel’s author has not offered a separate assessment.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: Russia and France: An Entente Cordiale, 1889–1900
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: Vasily Molodyakov
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: A useful companion: it shows how French money reached Port Arthur, and the title seems deliberately ambiguous.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: A historian of Japan and French nationalism traces the brief “golden age” of an alliance between autocratic empire and republic: Alexander III standing bareheaded for the Marseillaise at Kronstadt, Russian sailors in Toulon. Behind the romance lay calculation: France needed an ally against Germany, Russia needed money. For Dalny, the connection was direct: French capital established the Russo-Chinese Bank, which financed the Chinese Eastern Railway, and France joined Russia in forcing Japan to return Liaodong. The irony is that Paris remained neutral in 1904 and signed its own entente cordiale with London.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: Liaodong and Its Ports: Port Arthur and Dalianwan
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: Władysław Kotwicz, Leonid Borodovsky
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: Light reading with some curious details, and useful practice in pre-revolutionary Russian spelling.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: A 47-page booklet published by Orientalists in summer 1898, five months after the Kwantung lease, as an inexpensive alternative to the Finance Ministry’s costly Description of Manchuria. It describes the bay where Dalny would be founded a year later: ruined forts, one pier, a street five paces wide, Shin-tai’s bakery and living costs a third of Vladivostok’s, “but no amusements whatsoever”. The authors argued for “Guan-dong” instead of “Kwantung” and lost; their prediction that Dalianwan would become northern China’s equivalent of Shanghai and Hong Kong proved sound. Available in the National Electronic Library.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: Letters to My Neighbours, 1902–1904
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: Mikhail Menshikov
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: The elaborate prose takes effort, but century-old questions sound familiar.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: Columns by a leading journalist of the early twentieth century, a former naval navigator who wrote for Suvorin’s Novoye Vremya on finance, drinking, schools, Tolstoy, Chekhov and the war with Japan. The central wartime essay is “Internal Defence” from 1904. Instead of analysing manoeuvres at Liaoyang, Menshikov asks about the condition of the country fighting the war, arguing that defeats in Manchuria begin in offices, schools and taverns. His sermon-like newspaper prose demands patience, but rewards it.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: Anecdotes of the Russian Empire: The Russo-Japanese War
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: A. V. Shevchenko
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: An unlikely success: the commentary makes jokes from 1905 funny again.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: Wartime jokes about Stessel, who has “already surrendered”, the fleet, which is “in Japan”, and the turmoil left after Portsmouth. A footnote usually kills a joke, but here the commentary is so well judged that the joke begins to work: once you know who Stessel was and what was signed at Portsmouth, you can laugh with the morning-paper readers. Such texts show whom society distrusted and what it understood before official bulletins caught up.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: Cruisers
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: Valentin Pikul
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: A novel that can keep you awake until morning, with the proviso that you need a reference book to tell where Yegoryev ends and Pikul begins.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: The Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment seen through the fictional midshipman Panafidin: Bogatyr, Rurik, the battle with Kamimura’s squadron, a cruiser’s sinking, captivity and return to a shattered fleet. The real Trusov, Jessen, Bezobrazov and Kamimura appear alongside him, with Yegoryev’s 1939 study providing the foundation. Short, sharp sentences and fast scenes keep you reading until two in the morning. Historians’ objections are fair: the invented hero sinks with the real Rurik, the romance and staff rival are fabricated, and the ending tends towards nineteenth-century sentimentality. But afterwards you will stop confusing Rurik with Varyag.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: Port Arthur
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: Alexander Stepanov
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: Outdated as history, exemplary as a monument to Soviet fiction of the 1940s; read it to understand your grandfather’s firm views on Stessel.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: A Stalin Prize in 1946 and millions of copies: a volume of Port Arthur can be found in almost every Russian country house. It is a model novel of its era, with roles assigned in advance: generals sell out, soldiers fight to the death. Stessel and Fok betray the fortress for five million, though the court said nothing about a sale; Kondratenko is canonised, Kolchak serves on the wrong ship and the romance is crushingly heavy. The author’s own story is another matter: archival research published in 2010 found that neither he nor his father had been inside the besieged fortress. His actual wartime life was harsher than the legend.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: The Zvonaryov Family
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: Alexander Stepanov
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: The sequel to Port Arthur, where the “real horror” is only beginning.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: An unfinished sequel to Port Arthur, written in 1959–1963 and covering 1905–1916. Its opening chapters overflow with strikes, labour unrest and Bolshevism; politics fills every line. The love triangle survives: on the First World War front, Zvonaryov, by then the father of three daughters, meets Nadya again and is “overwhelmed” by feeling. The channel’s author read both novels and considers that a very brave act.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: The Crisis of Moral Consciousness in Russia and the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: A. L. Panishchev
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: Read it if you want an argument: “moral consciousness” here takes the place of shells rather than following them.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: The study begins with the premise that souls, rather than battleships, lost the war and fits the whole story to that claim. The war itself arrives only around page 50, after Alexander II’s reforms and a “crisis of messianism”; there are more mirrors in the chapter titles than at Versailles. Moral decline cannot be measured but can explain anything, so Shimose explosive, the single-track Trans-Siberian and Kuropatkin’s decisions recede. Port Arthur’s defence gets about ten pages, Japanese culture three. An important subject becomes a sermon illustrated with history.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: The Russo-Japanese War and the Bolsheviks’ Attitude towards It
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: Yemelyan Yaroslavsky
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: Little use for the war itself; revealing about how the USSR rewrote it.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: A 48-page booklet from the 1930s by a party historian and the country’s leading atheist. Its thesis is blunt: tsarism’s defeat “revolutionised the masses”, the Bolsheviks “favoured defeat”, and Port Arthur, Mukden and Tsushima made a useful prelude to 1905. Lenin, Stalin and proclamations supply the evidence. The irony lies in its afterlife: in 1945 Stalin would call the same defeat a “black stain” the country had waited forty years to erase. Read the booklet beside that speech to see one event’s meaning reversed. The 2020 reprint’s cover, with Stalin above a map of Asia, already indicates the approach.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: Ensigns of the Admiralty
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: Vladimir Poselyagin
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: A promise to rewrite the Russo-Japanese War produces boredom: it barely merits a facepalm.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: The first volume of The Twins trilogy. A modern person’s mind inhabits twin brothers who become universal soldiers before finishing naval school, murder British bankers to block Japanese loans and sink destroyers by the dozen at Port Arthur to Makarov’s fatherly praise. Stessel naturally betrays the fortress for money, villains come labelled, every twist is visible three chapters ahead and there is no ending. The prose sounds like a favourite dream retold in a garage, full of “anyway” and “so we got them”, with antisemitic motifs besides. The channel’s conclusion: reread the real history; its plot is better.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: Lieutenants of the Admiralty
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: Vladimir Poselyagin
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: Finished at 2.5× speed, and still a waste of time.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: The second part of The Twins. Vitgeft brings the squadron safely to Vladivostok and becomes naval minister; in reality, a shell hit on Tsesarevich left only part of his leg. Russia and Japan settle for a draw. The brothers then learn night vision and telekinesis, fight in every war on earth for ten years, avenge themselves on journalists and single-handedly replace the fleet in the First World War. Knowing the future, they try to prevent nothing: they simply grow rich and shoot. No building, no doubts, just resentment and endless gunfire. Again, no ending.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: On the Road to Collapse: The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905. A Military and Political History
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: Oleg Airapetov
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: The channel’s author recommends this as one of the best books in Russian for understanding the war as a whole.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: A military and political history from Russia’s advance into the Far East to the army’s return after the Treaty of Portsmouth. Port Arthur is placed alongside diplomacy, finance and decisions in St Petersburg. Conclusions draw on documents, memoirs and correspondence. Moscow: Algoritm, 2014. 496 pp. Historical Discoveries series.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: Russia and Japan: The Golden Age, 1905–1916
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: Vasily Molodyakov
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: Read after the books on the war; the reviewer questions the author’s “golden age” label.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: The rapprochement of former enemies after Portsmouth: the conventions of 1907, 1910 and 1912, spheres of influence in Manchuria, arms deliveries and the 1916 treaty. The review draws attention to the cost of this friendship for China, Korea and Mongolia. Moscow: Prospekt, 2025. 271 pp. Secrets of Friendship series.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: The Diamond Chariot
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: Boris Akunin
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: The channel’s author recommends this as a fictional introduction to the war and Japanese culture.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: The two parts of this Fandorin novel share an intrigue. In 1905 the hero investigates preparations for sabotage on the Trans-Siberian; in 1878 he serves as vice-consul in Yokohama, meeting Masa and encountering Japanese life. The post discusses an annotated edition. The fictional plot should be distinguished from documentary history.

src/i18n/en/books.json.title: Russia and the USSR in the Wars of the Twentieth Century: Armed Forces Losses. A Statistical Study
src/i18n/en/books.json.author: Edited by G. F. Krivosheev
src/i18n/en/books.json.verdict: For studying troop numbers and losses, with care over differing categories and counting sources.
src/i18n/en/books.json.annotation: A statistical study based on archival material. The post uses it to compare Port Arthur’s garrison and armaments, army and navy losses, the defenders’ condition at surrender and prisoner numbers. It cites several divergent estimates that cannot be treated as the same measure. Moscow: OLMA-Press, 2001.

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Nicholas II Alexandrovich
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Emperor under whom Russia leased Kwantung, founded Dalny and lost the war with Japan
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Born on 6 (18) May 1868 at Tsarskoye Selo, he came to the throne in 1894. As heir, he made his Eastern journey in 1890–1891; at Ōtsu on 11 May 1891 New Style, the policeman Tsuda Sanzō wounded his head with a sabre. On the return journey he inaugurated the Ussuri Railway at Vladivostok, the beginning of the Trans-Siberian. He directed Far Eastern policy personally: the Chinese Eastern Railway, the Kwantung lease in 1898, the Russian name Dalny for the new port, and the occupation of Manchuria in 1900. In 1903 he effectively removed ministers from Far Eastern affairs, establishing Alekseyev’s viceroyalty, backing Bezobrazov’s group and retiring Witte to an honorary post. He did not want war and long doubted Japan would dare fight, but the failure to withdraw from Manchuria and prolonged negotiations made it almost inevitable. The Treaty of Portsmouth transferred Kwantung, with Port Arthur and Dalny, to Japan. Nicholas pardoned Stessel in May 1909. He was executed with his family in Yekaterinburg in July 1918.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “God grant that the fears expressed here do not come true!” — annotation on N. I. Grodekov’s memorandum about another war with Japan

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Sergei Yulyevich Witte
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Finance minister, architect of the Chinese Eastern Railway project and founder of Dalny; signed the Treaty of Portsmouth
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Born in Tiflis in 1849, Witte graduated in physics and mathematics from Novorossiysk University and by 1886 managed the Southwestern Railways. In 1892 he became transport minister, then finance minister for eleven years: the state spirits monopoly, the gold ruble of 1897 and Trans-Siberian construction. In 1896 he negotiated with Li Hongzhang and secured the Chinese Eastern Railway concession. He opposed taking Port Arthur but arranged the lease once the decision was made. In Kwantung his main concern was Dalny, built with its port by the railway company using Finance Ministry money, while Port Arthur’s defences lacked funds. He toured Manchuria and visited Dalny in 1902. Removed as minister in August 1903, he negotiated at Portsmouth in 1905, avoiding an indemnity but conceding southern Sakhalin and the Kwantung lease to Japan. He gained a count’s title and the nickname “Count Half-Sakhalin”, and drafted the October Manifesto. He died on 28 February (13 March) 1915.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “That madman Bezobrazov has vanished, gone under” — Witte to Kuropatkin, 1904

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Yevgeny Ivanovich Alekseyev
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: First chief administrator of Kwantung; from 1903, Viceroy of the Far East, based in Port Arthur
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Born in 1843, officially the son of Lieutenant Commander Ivan Alekseyev, he was dogged by rumours that Alexander II was his father. After naval college he sailed around the world and served as naval attaché in Paris in the 1880s. He commanded the Pacific Fleet from 1895. In 1899 he became Kwantung’s first chief administrator, combining army, navy and civilian authority. The territory was divided into five districts, with Chinese officials retained as intermediaries. He directed Russian forces against the Boxers in 1900. As Far Eastern viceroy from August 1903, he oversaw negotiations with Japan, China and Korea. His instruction to avoid risks and preserve the squadron restricted the fleet at Port Arthur. He lost supreme command after the Shahe in October 1904; the viceroyalty was abolished in 1905. His rival Witte’s memoirs did much to shape his reputation. He died in Yalta on 27 May (9 June) 1917.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “He had sound judgment and a strong will” — naval historian V. Gribovsky on Alekseyev

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Li Hongzhang (李鸿章)
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Qing statesman who developed the Beiyang Fleet base at Lüshunkou and signed the Chinese Eastern Railway and Kwantung lease agreements
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Born in Hefei, Anhui, in 1823. From 1870 he spent almost a quarter-century governing the capital province of Zhili and overseeing northern ports, building arsenals, telegraphs, steamship companies and the Beiyang Fleet. In the 1880s, the fishing village of Lüshunkou became its base, with docks and batteries: the future Port Arthur, captured by Japan in a single day in 1894. At Shimonoseki, while negotiating peace in 1895, Li was wounded by a Japanese extremist, and Japan reduced the indemnity from 300 to 200 million taels. At Nicholas II’s coronation in 1896 he signed an alliance against Japan and agreed to the Chinese Eastern Railway; he was promised 3 million rubles. In spring 1898 he signed the Kwantung lease convention and received 500,000 rubles. As governor in Canton in 1900 he refused Cixi’s order to wage war on the powers; in 1901 he signed the Boxer Protocol. He died in Beijing in November 1901 without signing the Manchurian agreement sought by St Petersburg.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “Use barbarians to control barbarians” — a principle Li Hongzhang followed throughout his life

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Alexander Mikhailovich Bezobrazov
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: State secretary, leader of the “Bezobrazov circle” and the Yalu timber venture
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Born in 1853, or 1855 according to other sources, he retired as a captain in the Cavalier Guards. Grand Duke Alexander Mikhailovich introduced him to Nicholas II in 1898. Bezobrazov proposed a “peaceful conquest” of Korea through private enterprise modelled on the British East India Company. Its foundation was a timber concession on the Yalu and Tumen rivers, obtained by Vladivostok merchant Julius Briner in 1896 and purchased in 1898 against Witte’s opposition. Soldiers disguised as loggers went to the Yalu and built fortifications. Grand dukes, the dowager empress and the treasury supplied funds: 2 million rubles went to the concession in the first half of 1903. Bezobrazov became state secretary on 6 May 1903. That August Witte lost the Finance Ministry and Viceroy Alekseyev was instructed to discuss economic matters with Bezobrazov. He left for Switzerland in early 1904 and held no further role after 1905. He died in exile in Paris in 1931. Historians dispute whether he was a principal cause of the war or a convenient scapegoat.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “A great fantasist” with boundless self-confidence — V. I. Gurko on Bezobrazov

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Vyacheslav Konstantinovich von Plehve
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Interior minister in 1902–1904 and ally of Bezobrazov’s circle; the remark about a “small victorious war” is attributed to him
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Born in Meshchovsk, Kaluga province, in 1846, he graduated in law from Moscow University and worked in the prosecution service. After Alexander II’s assassination he headed the Police Department and crushed Narodnaya Volya, later serving as state secretary and pursuing Russification in Finland. He became interior minister in April 1902 after Sipyagin’s assassination. A rival of Witte, he supported Bezobrazov’s group; some historians regard him as its inspiration. The remark “we need a small victorious war” survives only at second hand, in a 1907 book under the pseudonym A. Morskoy and Witte’s memoirs, published in 1922. Witte had not heard it himself, quoting Kuropatkin; no independent confirmation exists. Plehve was killed by Socialist Revolutionary Yegor Sozonov’s bomb on Izmailovsky Avenue, St Petersburg, on 15 July 1904. Yevno Azef and Boris Savinkov directed the Combat Organisation’s operation. Two days later Japanese troops reached Port Arthur’s immediate approaches and the siege began.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “To hold back the revolution, we need a small victorious war” — words attributed to Plehve in Witte’s memoirs; authenticity unproven

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Alexei Nikolayevich Kuropatkin
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: War minister in 1898–1904, then commander of the Manchurian Army and commander-in-chief
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: War minister from 1898 to 1904, Kuropatkin opposed Witte’s policy of withdrawal from Manchuria. According to Witte, he welcomed the Boxer Rebellion as a pretext for occupation. In 1903 General D. I. Subotich wrote to him that Vladivostok was enough for Russia and its Manchurian policy would bring ruin. Kuropatkin took command of the Manchurian Army at the outbreak of war and succeeded Alekseyev as commander-in-chief after the Shahe in October 1904. The army retreated through the Yalu, Liaoyang, Shahe, Sandepu and Mukden in February–March 1905, after which he was removed. The headquarters’ 1905 album shows him thanking Putilov Hill’s heroes and inspecting a hospital train. His papers are in the Russian State Military Historical Archive, Collection 165. He deposited his diary for 1904–1906 in the military archive in autumn 1915 before leaving for the front; Krasny Arkhiv published it in 1922–1935. In 1913 he proposed moving the border so that the Gobi Desert would separate Russia from China.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “I am very glad. This will give us a pretext to seize Manchuria” — Kuropatkin on the Boxer Rebellion, as reported by Witte

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Roman Isidorovich Kondratenko
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Commander of Port Arthur’s land defences, the “soul of the defence”
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Born in Tiflis on 30 September (12 October) 1857, the tenth child of a retired major. He graduated from the Nikolayev Engineering School, Nikolayev Engineering Academy and General Staff Academy, finishing both academies in the first category. He commanded the 20th Rifle Regiment, with which he first saw Port Arthur in 1900. In November 1903 he took over the 7th East Siberian Rifle Brigade there; from the war’s start Stessel entrusted him with the entire land front. He completed defences under fire, installed guns from stores and ships, organised hand-grenade manufacture and supported inventors of mine throwers. On 18 September 1904 he warned Stessel not to expect timely relief; his letter went no further. He died with eight officers in Fort No. II’s officers’ casemate on 2 (15) December 1904, struck by an 11-inch shell. His remains were moved to the Alexander Nevsky Monastery in 1905. A Japanese memorial marks his death.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “No assault can be terrifying if we resolve to fulfil the oath we have sworn to the very end” — Kondratenko’s order after the fighting at the Wolf Hills, July 1904

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Anatoly Mikhailovich Stessel
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Commander of the Kwantung Fortified Region; signed Port Arthur’s surrender
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: During the war, Stessel commanded the Kwantung Fortified Region; K. N. Smirnov commanded the fortress, and R. I. Kondratenko led the land defences, entrusted with the whole land front from the first days. During the first assault Stessel wrote that Kondratenko should not accompany individual companies and asked him by telephone not to go into combat personally. He took no action on Kondratenko’s letter of 18 September 1904 proposing a truthful report to the tsar. On 20 December 1904 (2 January 1905), he signed the surrender against the military council’s decision to hold out. Around 23,000–25,000 men became prisoners. Sentenced to death for surrendering the fortress, he received a commuted sentence of ten years and was pardoned by Nicholas II in May 1909. The verdict contained no charge of selling the fortress, central to Stepanov’s Port Arthur. The defence’s most disputed figure, he inspired a 1905 joke: “Your turn to deal! — I’ve already surrendered.”
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “He must not be sent with individual companies. His loss would be irreplaceable” — Stessel on Kondratenko during the first assault

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Stepan Osipovich Makarov
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Fleet commander at Port Arthur in February–March 1904; died aboard Petropavlovsk
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Vice admiral, oceanographer and ship designer who initiated the icebreaker Yermak. He arrived at Port Arthur in late February 1904, replacing Vice Admiral O. V. Stark, under whom the squadron had been caught by the Japanese night attack. In 36 days of command he restored confidence and began taking the squadron to sea. On 10 March 1904 he appointed Rear Admiral K. P. Jessen to command the Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment. On 31 March (13 April), his flagship Petropavlovsk struck a mine and sank. Captain Lilje, who witnessed it, wrote that she disappeared “within some three minutes”. The admiral, around 650 crew and the painter Vasily Vereshchagin, aboard to make sketches, died; around 80 survived. Vitgeft succeeded him, and the squadron returned to the caution prescribed by the viceroy. In time-travel novels, Makarov usually survives.

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Wilhelm Karlovich Vitgeft
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: The viceroy’s naval chief of staff; commanded the First Squadron after Makarov and died in the Yellow Sea battle
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Rear admiral and naval chief of staff to Viceroy Alekseyev. Leaving a meeting on the evening of 26 January 1904, hours before the Japanese attack, he said extensive precautions for the squadron were unnecessary. Negotiations were still under way and war without a declaration seemed unthinkable. After Makarov’s death in April 1904 he effectively took command. An experienced staff officer, he did not consider himself a fleet commander; the viceroy’s injunction to avoid risk and preserve the squadron reinforced his caution. On 28 July (10 August) 1904, directly ordered from St Petersburg, he attempted to break through to Vladivostok. A Japanese shell struck the bridge of his flagship Tsesarevich during the Yellow Sea battle and killed him. With damaged steering, Tsesarevich circled and broke the formation, leaving the squadron without effective command. Some ships were interned at Qingdao, Shanghai and Saigon; the main force returned to Port Arthur to be destroyed later by siege howitzers. None reached Vladivostok.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “…since there will be no war” — Vitgeft on the evening of 26 January 1904, hours before the Japanese destroyer attack

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Konstantin Ivanovich Velichko
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Military engineer who designed Port Arthur’s land defences
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Military engineer, fortification specialist and professor at the Nikolayev Engineering Academy. In 1898–1900 he designed Port Arthur’s system of forts and intermediate works, approved on 18 January 1900. It included six forts, I–VI, as heavily armed strongpoints with garrisons of up to two companies, and five intermediate fortifications held mainly by infantry. Only about 4.25 million of the budgeted 15 million rubles was provided before the war. Velichko reduced concrete thickness: shelter vaults reached 0.9 metres, designed against 6-inch shells. Planning for a garrison no larger than 11,300, he placed the line a few kilometres from town, leaving several heights outside it, including 203 Metre Hill. The land-front forts were unfinished when war began; Fort VI remained on paper. The design was later criticised, but in 1900 neither a months-long siege nor 280 mm howitzers had been anticipated.

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Vladimir Vasilyevich Sakharov
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Engineer who built Dalny’s port and became its first city governor
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: A harbour engineer who built Vladivostok’s commercial port before coming to Kwantung. From 1899 he designed and built the port in Victoria Bay, within Dalian Bay, then became Dalny’s city governor. The Chinese Eastern Railway Company built port and city; the first harbour phase cost 10.8 million rubles, and within three years Dalny ranked second in China for cargo turnover, after Shanghai. The city gained Manchuria’s first power station, water mains and a telephone network. At the outbreak of war, State Councillor Sakharov volunteered for Port Arthur. A caption to his 1904 magazine portrait says he served as a captain under General Fok and contributed much to the defence through his ingenuity. He died of typhus in the fortress in October 1904, aged 45. The Japanese captured his port almost intact in May 1904 and used it to supply the siege army, then developed Dairen along the Russian plan for forty years.

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Kazimierz Geliodorovich Skolimowski
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Architect of Dalny’s general plan
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Polish architect who designed Dalny’s general plan. Born in Brodnia near Łódź in 1862, he studied at St Petersburg’s Academy of Arts and in Berlin and Munich. In 1899, on Alexander Pomerantsev’s recommendation, he was invited to design Dalny. Rejecting a rectangular grid, he proposed a radial layout: circular Nikolayevskaya Square, 213 metres across, with ten avenues. He presented a new general plan in 1900 and detailed design in 1903, considering terrain, street views and living conditions. A park separated the European and Chinese towns. His report “On Designing the Plan of the City of Dalny” was delivered on 3 (16) February 1904 and published in Zodchiy, Nos. 12–14. Returning to Poland, he became Kalisz’s city architect. He died on 28 December 1923 while inspecting the icy roof of the town hall under construction. His radial layout still shapes central Dalian.
src/i18n/en/people.json.portrait_note: Portrait from the channel’s new post. Patronymic and life dates updated from the publication of 11 November 2026.

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Mikhail Ivanovich Lilje
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Military engineer who built Kwantung’s fortifications and wrote the Diary of the Siege of Port Arthur
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Born into a noble family in 1868, Lilje graduated from the Nikolayev Engineering Academy and was posted to Port Arthur in 1898. From 1900 he directed construction for the Kwantung Engineering Administration, building the works he would later defend. He kept a diary throughout the siege, from January 1904 to January 1905. On the first night he wrote that the squadron was “completely unprepared for battle”; on 31 March he witnessed Petropavlovsk’s sinking. In November he recorded scurvy and command disputes, calling 203 Metre Hill “Arthur’s Calvary”. On 20 December he explained the night’s explosions: “Our sailors were blowing up all our ships, cranes, and so on.” Decorated after the war with the Orders of St Anne and St Vladimir with swords, he became a lieutenant colonel and built defences in Finland during the First World War. He emigrated to France after 1917 and died in 1941. He sent his manuscript to the USSR, where it was held in the Lenin Library, nearly lost during preparations for a 1992 edition and finally published from a surviving copy in 2002.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “All this muddle vividly illustrates our order and preparedness for war” — diary, 28 January 1904

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Nogi Maresuke
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Commander of the Japanese Third Army, which besieged Port Arthur
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Japanese general commanding the Third Army, which conducted Port Arthur’s land siege from summer 1904. Foreign war correspondents worked at his headquarters: on the first assault’s morning he received them and asked an interpreter to state each man’s nationality and credentials. The army made four general assaults; Russian estimates put Japan’s losses at Port Arthur above 110,000. Nogi lost both sons in the campaign. After the failed August assault, 280 mm howitzers were brought from Japanese coastal fortresses and began firing in late September 1904. On 22 November (5 December), the army took 203 Metre Hill, enabling siege artillery to destroy the squadron in the harbour’s inner basins. The fortress surrendered on 20 December 1904 (2 January 1905). Nogi and his wife died by suicide on the day of Emperor Meiji’s funeral in 1912.

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Karl Petrovich Jessen
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Commander of the Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment, whose raids interrupted the delivery of siege howitzers to Port Arthur
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Rear admiral appointed by Makarov on 10 March 1904 to command the Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment: Rossiya, Gromoboi, Rurik and Bogatyr. Its task was to attack Japanese trade and communications with Korea. On 2 (15) June, under temporary commander Vice Admiral P. A. Bezobrazov, the cruisers sank Hitachi Maru and Izumi Maru in the Korea Strait; Sado Maru ran aground. Hitachi Maru and Sado Maru carried 18 siege howitzers of 280 mm for Port Arthur. In July Jessen raided Japan’s eastern coast and sank the British steamer Knight Commander 15 miles from the entrance to Tokyo Bay; a London prize court upheld the capture. On 1 (14) August off Ulsan, the detachment, sailing to meet the squadron attempting to escape Port Arthur, encountered Kamimura’s cruisers and lost Rurik. Jessen received the Order of St George, 4th Class, and brought the surviving ships to the Baltic after the war. He was subsequently reprimanded, faced trial and retired in 1908.

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Kamimura Hikonojō
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Japanese vice admiral who commanded the cruisers opposing the Vladivostok detachment
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Japanese vice admiral commanding an armoured-cruiser squadron. His main task in 1904 was to counter the Vladivostok cruisers, which attacked Japanese transports in the Sea of Japan and off Japan’s Pacific coast. On 2 (15) June, Russian cruisers sank transports carrying 280 mm siege howitzers for the army at Port Arthur; the Japanese navy had to commit an entire squadron against Vladivostok. On 1 (14) August off Ulsan, Kamimura intercepted Jessen’s force as it sailed to meet the squadron breaking out of Port Arthur. Hits to Rurik’s stern disabled her steering; she fell behind and was scuttled. More than 200 died, while the Japanese rescued around 625 sailors. Rossiya and Gromoboi returned to Vladivostok badly damaged, effectively ending the cruiser campaign. Kamimura is a historical character in Valentin Pikul’s Cruisers.

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Dean Ivanovich Subotich
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: An early administrator of Kwantung, later Governor-General of the Amur region; proposed returning Dalny and Port Arthur to China
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: A general of Serbian origin. In the first year of the Russian lease he headed Kwantung after Admiral F. V. Dubasov, until authority passed to Y. I. Alekseyev in 1899. He later succeeded N. I. Grodekov as Governor-General of the Amur region. In 1903, months before the war, he sent War Minister Kuropatkin a memorandum historian M. V. Khodyakov considers the most clear-headed of the generals’ Manchurian plans. Subotich argued that Russia was a land power and Vladivostok was sufficient. A verst of the Chinese Eastern Railway cost 152,000 rubles, 80,000 more than in Transbaikalia; at least a billion had been invested in Manchuria. He proposed a deal modelled on the sale of Alaska: return southern Manchuria, including Dalny and Port Arthur, to China in exchange for northern Manchuria. Two years later Russia lost Dalny and Port Arthur to Japan under the Treaty of Portsmouth.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: Russia is heading “rather towards ruin and exhaustion” — Subotich’s memorandum to Kuropatkin, 1903

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Alexander Nikolayevich Stepanov
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Author of Port Arthur, awarded the Stalin Prize in 1946
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Born in Odessa in 1892 into a family of hereditary artillerymen. He graduated from the Sumy Cadet Corps and Mikhailovsky Artillery School, serving in the First World War with the Life Guards Rifle Artillery Battalion. He received six orders and, in February 1915, the St George Sword for fighting near Rudka-Skruda. He assembled Port Arthur from memoirs, veterans’ letters and his own front-line experience. The novel ran to 17 editions and over a million copies, receiving the Stalin Prize, First Class, in 1946. Stessel and Fok are traitors selling the fortress; Kondratenko is its last support. This scheme shaped popular views of the defence for decades. Stepanov claimed to have survived the siege as a boy at his father’s Electric Cliff battery, but in 2010 D. K. Nikolayev and O. V. Chistyakov demonstrated from archives that neither had been in the fortress. He died in 1965 and was buried at Novodevichy Cemetery.

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Valentin Savvich Pikul
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Author of Cruisers, a novel about the Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Born in Leningrad on 13 July 1928, Pikul survived the siege’s first winter, graduated from the Solovki naval boys’ school in 1943 and served on the Northern Fleet destroyer Grozny until the war ended. Apart from a year at a naval preparatory school, he received no further education. He lived in Riga from 1962. His historical novels appeared in more than 500 editions, totalling around half a billion copies. Cruisers, written in 38 days for the Tsushima anniversary in 1985, received the Gorky State Prize of the RSFSR in 1988. It drew on V. Ye. Yegoryev’s 1939 study of Vladivostok cruiser operations. Historical figures Trusov, Dabich, Stemman, Jessen, P. A. Bezobrazov, Reitzenstein and Kamimura appear beside the invented midshipman Panafidin, who sinks with the real Rurik. Historians criticise this blending of fiction and documentary material. Pikul died in Riga on 16 July 1990.

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Vikenty Vikentyevich Veresayev (Smidovich)
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Military doctor in Manchuria and author of In the Russo-Japanese War
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Born in Tula in 1867, he graduated in history and philology from St Petersburg University and in medicine from Dorpat. His 1901 Notes of a Doctor caused a scandal through its frank account of medical errors and experiments on patients. Called from the reserve in 1904, he went to Manchuria as an army doctor and followed a field hospital through the whole war, including Mukden and the retreat, returning through revolutionary Siberia. In the Russo-Japanese War describes hospitals without patients, wounded men transported aimlessly for weeks, bureaucracy, the Mukden retreat and rallies at Trans-Siberian stations. Contemporaries accused him of being unpatriotic. Chapters appeared soon after the war; the full book in 1928. During the First World War he headed a military medical unit. Later he compiled Pushkin in Life and Gogol in Life and translated the Iliad and Odyssey. He received the Stalin Prize in 1943 and died in Moscow in June 1945.

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Yevgeny Sergeyevich Botkin
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Red Cross doctor with the Manchurian Army and author of Light and Shadows of the Russo-Japanese War
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Son of the physician S. P. Botkin, a doctor of medicine and lecturer at the Military Medical Academy. At the war’s outbreak he volunteered for Manchuria and headed the Red Cross medical service with the army in the field. Under shrapnel at Wafangou, now Wafangdian within Dalian, he carried wounded men and gave them his horse. For courage under fire he received military orders, including St Vladimir, 3rd and 2nd Class with swords. His letters to his wife appeared in Vestnik Evropy in 1908 and then as a book. Alongside dressing stations, typhus and dysentery that killed doctors and nurses, they contain observations of Manchurian life: counting and etiquette, houses, theatre and Mukden’s imperial tombs. In 1908 he became Nicholas II’s physician, followed the family into exile and was executed with them at the Ipatiev House in July 1918. The Russian Orthodox Church canonised him in 2016.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “Now we feel war around us as one feels death in the house of a hopelessly ill patient” — letters to his wife

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Leo Nikolayevich Tolstoy
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Author of the anti-war essay Bethink Yourselves! (1904)
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: In early 1904, as prayers and patriotic demonstrations greeted the war, the 75-year-old Tolstoy, who had defended Sevastopol’s Fourth Bastion in his youth, began Bethink Yourselves! It was ready by May. He wrote of peasants sent ten thousand versts to die for foreign land, priests blessing weapons, those stirring enthusiasm while remaining safe, and the soldier explaining his choice with “what else can you do?” The tsar appears more as an unhappy young man trapped in his own power. Tolstoy’s answer was for each person to heed their conscience and refuse to take part in killing. Russian newspapers rejected the essay. V. G. Chertkov sent it to England and The Times published it on 27 June (9 July) 1904. Moskovskiye Vedomosti replied with “The Maniac of Yasnaya Polyana”; Japan’s Heimin Shimbun translated it in August. The writer’s son Andrei volunteered for the war.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “War again. Again sufferings needless and unprovoked, again lies, again universal stupefaction and the brutalisation of men” — opening of Bethink Yourselves!

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Konstantin Dmitriyevich Balmont
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Poet whose Our Tsar (1906) reduces the reign to Mukden and Tsushima
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Born in Vladimir province on 15 June 1867, Balmont was expelled from Shuya Gymnasium and Moscow University for involvement in political circles. In Boundlessness (1895), Burning Buildings (1900) and Let Us Be Like the Sun (1903) made him a leading Russian Symbolist. His poem “The Little Sultan” brought a two-year ban from capitals and university towns in 1901. The Japanese war and the 1905 revolution completed his politicisation. He left illegally for Paris in late 1905 and wrote “Our Tsar” in 1906. The reign is reduced to Mukden and Tsushima, beginning at Khodynka and destined to end on the scaffold. The poem appeared in Songs of an Avenger, Paris, 1907, but not in Russia. Balmont returned on 5 May 1913 under the Romanov tercentenary amnesty, visited Japan in 1916 and translated much tanka and haiku. Rejecting the October Revolution, he left for France in 1920 and died at Noisy-le-Grand near Paris on 23 December 1942.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “Our tsar is Mukden, our tsar is Tsushima, / Our tsar is a bloody stain” — Our Tsar, 1906

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Mikhail Osipovich Menshikov
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Novoye Vremya journalist who wrote of the war as a test of the whole country
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: A graduate of Kronstadt’s naval technical school, Menshikov served as navigator and hydrographer, compiling sailing directions before turning to journalism. When Nedelya closed, A. S. Suvorin recruited him to Novoye Vremya. His Letters to My Neighbours appeared two or three times weekly until spring 1917; subscribers received monthly booklets to bind into annual volumes. The 1902–1904 collection spans the Russo-Japanese War. In “Internal Defence” (1904), he wrote about the country’s condition rather than manoeuvres near Liaoyang: peacetime patriotism had fallen dangerously low, though it had not died. National existence, he argued, “must be defended beyond the fields of Manchuria”; defeats began at home, in offices, schools and taverns. He regarded the war as an examination the country had failed. Arrested at Valdai on 19 September 1918, he was shot without trial the next day.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “The thunder of war was needed to wake our consciousness” — Internal Defence, 1904

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Ilya Alexeyevich Shatrov
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Bandmaster of the Mokshan Regiment and composer of On the Hills of Manchuria
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Son of a retired non-commissioned officer from Zemlyansk, Voronezh province; sources give his birth year as either 1879 or 1885. Bandmaster of the 214th Mokshan Infantry Regiment. In February 1905 near Mukden, with the regiment surrounded and ammunition running low, Colonel Pobyvanets ordered the colours and band forward. Shatrov led the musicians onto the parapet; they played a march under fire as the regiment broke through with bayonets. Seven hundred of four thousand men escaped; seven of 61 musicians survived, and Pobyvanets died. A year later at Zlatoust, Shatrov wrote The Mokshan Regiment on the Hills of Manchuria in their memory. Its first performance in Samara in spring 1908 met a cool response, but the score was reprinted 82 times in three years. Skitalets, S. Petrov, wrote the first lyrics. Shatrov later served with Red Army bands, returned to uniform in March 1945 and spent his final years conducting at Tambov’s Suvorov Military School. Promoted to Guards major on 20 April 1952, he died on 2 May that year.
src/i18n/en/people.json.quote: “Colours and band to the front!” — Colonel Pobyvanets’s order near Mukden, February 1905

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Sergei Mikhailovich Prokudin-Gorsky
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Photographer and printer who compiled and printed The Russo-Japanese War, 1904–1905 album
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: A pioneer of Russian colour photography, producing more than 2,600 images in 1905–1915. The US Library of Congress acquired most from his sons in 1948. His connection with the Russo-Japanese War is often misunderstood: he is widely believed to have photographed Manchuria himself in 1904. In fact, on a General Staff commission, he prepared for printing The Russo-Japanese War, 1904–1905, published by the commander-in-chief’s headquarters in 1905: around 300 plates photographed by others. It shows the war from Manchurian army headquarters: Shahe fighting, Putilov Hill, XVII Corps positions, Rennenkampf’s detachment and the retreat from Mukden to Tieling. His workshops also printed the Album of the Wartime Life of the XVII Army Corps, 54 plates and 231 photographic reproductions, compiled by the Corps of Military Topographers. His contribution to both was printing; others took the pictures.

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: William Arthur
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: British naval officer after whom Lüshunkou harbour was named Port Arthur
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: A Royal Navy lieutenant who took command of the gunboat HMS Algerine in June 1858 during the Second Opium War. The damaged vessel was towed into a small, unfortified fishing harbour where Arthur found shelter and charted the area. He did not name it himself: in August 1860 John Ward, commanding HMS Actaeon, named it after the lieutenant whose Algerine had been the first British ship to enter. The name took hold among the British and was adopted by Russia and other Western powers. After the lease of 1898 the fortress remained Port Arthur, although Nicholas II gave the neighbouring port the Russian name Dalny. The Chinese name Lüshunkou, “bay of smooth sailing”, traditionally dates to 1371. Arthur died in 1886, eighteen years before the siege. The claim that the port honoured Queen Victoria’s son Prince Arthur is not supported by documents.

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Mikhail Yevgenyevich Mühlberg
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: “Port Arthur’s smallest child”, born in the besieged fortress
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Born in besieged Port Arthur on 13 November 1904, baptised the day after the surrender, Mikhail lived 52 days. He was buried in the Russian cemetery at Goshinji Temple, Nagasaki, where an unassuming grey stone still bears his inscription. His father, Second Lieutenant Yevgeny Mühlberg, was wounded in the defence and received the Order of St George. His grandmother worked in a hospital throughout the siege and became his godmother. Historian Dmitry Nikolayev reconstructed the family’s life through parish registers and archives in “Misha from Nagasaki”, Rodina, 2016, following its later history too. Officers’ families lived beside the garrison inside the fortress: women worked in hospitals and children were born under fire.

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Vasily Vasilyevich Vereshchagin
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Battle painter who died aboard Petropavlovsk with Admiral Makarov
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: Born in Cherepovets, Vereshchagin graduated from the Naval Cadet Corps but chose the Academy of Arts over naval service. His paintings showed war through death and human suffering; he painted The Apotheosis of War in 1871. In 1874 he declined a professorship at the Academy. Working in Japan in autumn 1903, he painted Nikkō’s temples and warned of Russia’s unreadiness for war. He arrived at Port Arthur in spring 1904 and died on 31 March (13 April) when Petropavlovsk struck a mine. His body was not found.

src/i18n/en/people.json.name: Alexander Viktorovich Fok
src/i18n/en/people.json.role: Commander of the 4th East Siberian Rifle Division; succeeded Kondratenko as head of the fortress’s land defences
src/i18n/en/people.json.bio: A graduate of the Novgorod Arakcheyev Cadet Corps and Konstantinovsky Military School. He received the Order of St George, 4th Class, for crossing the Danube at Sistova in 1877 and served in the Chinese campaign of 1900–1901. In the Russo-Japanese War he commanded the 4th East Siberian Rifle Division; his actions at Jinzhou and unused reserves became disputed. During the siege he circulated staff “notes” offering advice and sharply criticising colleagues. After Kondratenko’s death, Stessel appointed him commander of the land defences. At the 1908 trial he was acquitted of the principal charges; a reprimand over the notes was dropped under the statute of limitations. He wounded Commandant Smirnov in a duel. He served with the Bulgarian army in 1912–1913 and lived in Bulgaria after the revolution. He died in 1926 and was buried near Svishtov.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: 203 Metre Hill
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 203高地 (203 Gāodì); Japanese monument: 尔灵山 (Ěrlíngshān)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: The 203 memorial area on the fortress’s western front, with a cherry garden at its foot
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A height behind the main line of forts, left without permanent defences in Velichko’s plan. Japanese troops assaulted it for a week from 15 November 1904. Its garrison lost around 5,000 men before abandoning it on 22 November (5 December). The summit overlooked the inner basins, allowing siege howitzers to sink the squadron at its moorings within days. Today a Japanese rifle-bullet-shaped monument, Erlingshan, whose name echoes “203”, stands on top. Sections of trenches survive, and the place where General Nogi’s son died is marked. Views extend over the harbour and western Lüshun.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: There is parking at the entrance (203景区停车场). Admission is paid; check prices and hours locally. Travel agencies quoted 30 yuan in 2025. Prices may differ during the spring cherry-blossom season.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Fort No. II (North Fort of East Jiguan Shan)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 东鸡冠山北堡垒 (Dōng Jīguānshān běi bǎolěi)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Dongjiguanshan visitor area, with the fort ruins and the Lüshun Russo-Japanese War Exhibition Hall (旅顺日俄战争陈列馆)
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A strongpoint on the northeastern front, where fighting for the counterscarp gallery continued for weeks, including underground. On 2 (15) December 1904, an 11-inch howitzer shell struck the officers’ casemate where General Roman Kondratenko was present; eight officers died with him. Three days later, on 18 December New Style, the Japanese blew up the parapet and captured the fort. The shattered casemates, ditch and caponiers remain visible. A stone erected by the Japanese marks the general’s death: “Place where Russian Major General Kondratenko fell.” A small museum stands nearby.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: Ctrip gives opening hours of 07:30–17:00. Admission is paid; travel agencies quote 25 yuan. Parking is at the entrance (东鸡冠山停车场). Check hours before travelling.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: The Great Eagle’s Nest
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 望台炮台 (Wàngtái pàotái)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A height with a Japanese memorial marker and viewpoint beside Jiguan Shan Road
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A hilltop battery between Forts II and III on the northeastern front. Its fall on 19 December 1904 (1 January 1905 New Style) was the defence’s last major event: that same day Stessel sent the Japanese an offer to surrender. Old guns and a memorial marker now stand on the summit, with views along the hills from Jiguan Shan to Erlongshan. The identification of the Russian name with the Chinese Wangtai is generally accepted, but should be checked against the 1904 fortress plan.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Fort No. III
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 二龙山堡垒 (Èrlóngshān bǎolěi)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Fort ruins on Erlongshan
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A fort on the northern front, on Erlongshan west of the Great Eagle’s Nest. Japanese troops drove mine galleries towards it and captured it on 15 (28) December 1904 after blowing up the parapet. Parts of the ditch and concrete structures survive. The coordinates mark the hilltop; the fort itself lies on the slope, so its exact position needs checking on site.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Fortification No. 3
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 松树山堡垒 (Sōngshùshān bǎolěi)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Fortification ruins on Songshushan
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: An intermediate work between the northern-front forts, built to the same basic scheme: rampart, dry ditch, caponiers and barracks. It fell on 18 (31) December 1904 after a Japanese mine beneath the parapet brought down a casemate. Ruins among pine trees and the explosion crater remain. It receives noticeably fewer visitors than 203 Metre Hill or Dongjiguanshan.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Fortification No. 5
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 鸦户嘴 (Yāhùzuǐ); signs call it the “Russian Army Command Fort”
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A surviving fortification in woodland, with a museum room, fortress model and coastal gun
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: An intermediate work on the western front between Forts V and VI. A published readiness memo reports Fortification No. 5 complete by 1 December 1903, while work on Fort VI had only just begun. According to the channel, Qing works preceded the Russian rebuilding after 1898; the precise sequence still needs verification. The channel reports no separate assault. The work was handed over at the capitulation, but had taken part in artillery action recorded in G. S. Pilsudski’s diary. Surviving features include rampart, dry ditch, caponiers, barracks and underground passages. The site displays a gun that the field report author identifies as a 10-inch coastal gun on a Durlacher mounting; its provenance is unestablished. A small museum room displays a fortress model and soldiers’ everyday life. The claim that 203 Metre Hill was commanded from here is not supported by documents.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: A quiet site that is not yet a regular tourist stop. The channel gives 38.7970, 121.1933 for navigation. Check access arrangements and whether a ticket is needed in advance.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Electric Cliff Battery
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 电岩炮台 (Diànyán pàotái)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A coastal battery memorial above the Yellow Sea
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A coastal battery on a cliff east of Golden Hill, named after a searchlight stationed there. It held 10-inch guns on Durlacher mountings, like the gun at Fortification No. 5. The battery covered the harbour entrance and fired on the Japanese fleet from the war’s first days. Today its concrete gun emplacements overlook the sea and the entrance to Lüshun harbour.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: One travel-agency account says foreigners cannot visit; other sources describe a normal paid attraction costing about 15 yuan. Check before travelling.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Golden Hill
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 黄金山 (Huángjīnshān)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Hill at the entrance to Lüshun harbour, partly within a military zone
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: The eastern side of the harbour entrance, sheltering the inner basins from the sea together with Tiger’s Tail peninsula. Grand Duke Kirill Vladimirovich raised the Russian flag above Golden Hill on 16 (28) March 1898. Coastal batteries built under the Qing and rebuilt by the Russians stood here. Below it, on the outer roadstead, the squadron was attacked by Japanese destroyers on 27 January (9 February) 1904. A town beach is now at its foot; military installations occupy the summit.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Quail Hill (Baiyushan)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 白玉山 (Báiyùshān)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Hilltop park with a Japanese tower from 1909 (白玉山塔), harbour views and a cable car
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: The hill above the Eastern Basin between the Old and New Towns, from which panoramas of Russian Port Arthur were photographed. After the war, at Nogi and Tōgō’s initiative, the Japanese built the roughly 67 m Hyōchūtō, or “Loyalty Tower”, now 白玉山塔. The viewpoint overlooks the inner harbour, Golden Hill, Tiger’s Tail and the land-front hills, making it a useful place to begin a visit to Lüshun.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: A road and cable car (白玉山索道) reach the summit. Ticket reports differ: travel agencies variously quote 40 yuan admission or a free tower with a paid cable car. Check locally.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Port Arthur’s Inner Harbour (Eastern and Western Basins)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 旅顺港 (Lǚshùn gǎng); 旅顺口 (Lǚshùnkǒu)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: An active PLA Navy base, with a public waterfront and viewpoints beside the town
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: Russia leased Kwantung for this harbour. Its narrow, deep entrance lies between Golden Hill and Tiger’s Tail, with two basins inside. The First Pacific Squadron was based here: seven battleships, cruisers and destroyers. After the loss of 203 Metre Hill, siege howitzers sank the ships beside the quays; only Sevastopol escaped, taken by Essen to White Wolf Bay. Today this is an active naval base. The civilian town reaches the water; the rest is viewed from Quail Hill. The coordinate is a representative point over the Eastern Basin.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: The base is closed to visitors. Photographing warships is not recommended.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Port Arthur Railway Station
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 旅顺站 (Lǚshùn zhàn)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A Russian-style wooden station on the waterfront; regular services have ended
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: Terminus of the Chinese Eastern Railway’s southern branch. Construction began around 1900 and the station opened in 1903. The wooden building with its green tented roof stands beside the Western Basin, one of Lüshun’s most photographed sights. The building’s history is tangled: some sources describe a Japanese rebuilding in 1905–1908, others a reconstruction from old drawings in the 2000s. Trains no longer run here. Metro Line 12 serves a different station, Lüshun, north of the centre.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: View the building from outside. The waterfront and the Quail Hill cable-car entrance are nearby.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Port Arthur Prison
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 旅顺日俄监狱旧址 (Lǚshùn Rì-É jiānyù jiùzhǐ)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: The Former Russo-Japanese Prison museum
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: The Russians began building the prison in 1902; the Japanese enlarged it in 1907. Brickwork reveals the difference: the grey blocks by the entrance are Russian, the large red blocks Japanese. Under Japanese rule it held Chinese, Korean and Japanese prisoners. Korean independence activist An Jung-geun, who killed Itō Hirobumi, was executed here in 1910. The prison operated until 1945 and became a museum in 1971. Cells, workshops and the execution site survive.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: Travel agencies in 2026 report free admission and Monday closure. We have not found official confirmation; check before visiting.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Port Arthur Russian and Soviet Military Cemetery
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 旅顺苏军烈士陵园 (Lǚshùn Sūjūn lièshì língyuán)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Soviet military memorial cemetery in Sanliqiao, with burials from 1904–1905 in the older section
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: One of the largest Russian military cemeteries outside Russia. Founded during the Russian period, it was landscaped by the Japanese authorities after the war as a memorial to the fortress’s fallen defenders. The older section consists mainly of mass graves from 1904, with a chapel and monument. From 1945, Soviet servicemen who died in Port Arthur were buried here, followed by casualties of the Korean War. A 1955 Soviet military monument stands at the entrance. Russian specialists restored the cemetery in the 2000s. General Kondratenko is not buried here: his remains were taken to St Petersburg in 1905.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Lüshun Museum
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 旅顺博物馆 (Lǚshùn bówùguǎn)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A state museum in the New Town (Taiyanggou)
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: Opened under Japanese administration in 1915 as an exhibition of local products and in 1917 as the Kwantung Government-General’s Museum of Manchurian and Mongolian Products. Its eclectic building combines European forms with Eastern details. Soviet troops transferred the museum to China on 1 February 1951. Collections now include archaeology, bronzes, calligraphy and material from Xinjiang. Local tradition says construction began under Russian rule; we have not found documentary confirmation.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Port Arthur’s New Town
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 太阳沟 (Tàiyánggōu)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: The historic Taiyanggou district: quiet streets of Russian and Japanese villas
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: The Russians laid out the New Town west of the harbour with straight, European-style streets; the channel mentions Morskaya and Pushkinskaya. Japanese administrative buildings followed. Russian villas, including one marked as a senior official’s residence (俄式高官住宅), now stand beside the former Kwantung Army headquarters, Lüshun Museum and the Soviet friendship tower. Trees line the streets, with black locust blossom in May.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: Allow 1–1.5 hours to walk the district’s streets from Lüshun Museum.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Sino-Soviet Friendship Tower
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 中苏友谊纪念塔 (Zhōng-Sū yǒuyì jìniàntǎ)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A monument on the square beside Lüshun Museum
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A monument of the 1950s, begun in 1955 and completed later according to differing sources. It commemorates Sino-Soviet friendship during the years when Port Arthur was a joint naval base, until 1955. It stands on a circular square beside Lüshun Museum in the New Town. Reliefs depict episodes from the two countries’ shared history.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: The square is open; view the monument from outside.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: The Meeting House at Shuishiying
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 水师营会见所旧址 (Shuǐshīyíng huìjiànsuǒ jiùzhǐ)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A memorial house on Lüshun’s northern outskirts
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A farmhouse in Shuishiying village where Generals Stessel and Nogi met on 23 December 1904 (5 January 1905 New Style), after the surrender had been signed. According to a familiar account, the horse Stessel gave Nogi was tied to a tree in the yard. The meeting entered a Japanese school song. The present house appears to be a reconstruction; its fidelity to the original needs checking.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Longwangtang: The Reservoir Cherry Garden
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 龙王塘樱花园 (Lóngwángtáng yīnghuā yuán)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A cherry-blossom park beside Longwangtang Reservoir (龙王塘水库)
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A park beside a reservoir built under Japanese rule between Dalian and Lüshun. Japanese settlers planted cherry trees here; it is now the best-known blossom spot near Dalian. Single-flowered varieties open around mid-April, doubles roughly a week later, with flowering continuing to the end of the month. The garden at 203 Metre Hill blooms about a week later. The coordinate is approximate: the park is below the dam at the reservoir’s southern end.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: A seasonal park with paid admission: travel agencies quoted 20 yuan in 2025. Excursion buses run from Dalian during the blossom season.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Nikolayevskaya Square
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 中山广场 (Zhōngshān guǎngchǎng)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Zhongshan Square in central Dalian, a circular square surrounded by Japanese-era banks and a hotel
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: The centre of Kazimierz Skolimowski’s plan: a circle 213 m across, with ten radiating streets, modelled on Paris’s Place de l’Étoile. The Russians laid out the square but did not build around it. The Japanese called it Ōhiroba, “Great Square”, and added banks, city hall, police headquarters and the Yamato Hotel between 1908 and 1936. Eight pre-war buildings survive; the British consulate was demolished in 1995. After 1945 the square was named for Sun Yat-sen.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: Metro: Zhongshan Square station (中山广场站). The square is open around the clock; buildings are illuminated in the evening.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Russian Street (Formerly Inzhenernaya)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 团结街 / 俄罗斯风情街 (Tuánjié jiē / Éluósī fēngqíng jiē)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A pedestrian tourist street in the former Russian administrative quarter
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A street in Dalny’s earliest district, north of the railway, where the administrative quarter was built in 1899–1902. The channel identifies former Inzhenernaya Street with today’s Russian Street. Some houses are original; much was added or restored in an “old-fashioned” style when the street became a tourist attraction. Souvenir shops occupy ground floors. Dalny’s city administration building stands at the far end.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: A 15–20 minute walk from Zhongshan Square across Victory Bridge. The street is always open.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Dalny City Administration Building
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 达里尼市政厅旧址 (Dálǐní shìzhèngtīng jiùzhǐ)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A historic building at the northern end of Russian Street
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: One of Dalny’s first masonry buildings, erected for the city administration in the early 1900s. Vladimir Sakharov, engineer, port builder and first city governor, administered Dalny from here. He volunteered for Port Arthur in 1904 and died there of typhus. Japanese institutions occupied the building after 1905; it later housed Dalian’s Natural History Museum for many years. It is now a protected monument, though the museum inside may be closed.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: The 1902 Building by the Bridge (Chinese Eastern Railway Office)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 大连艺术展览馆 / 大连美术馆 (Dàlián yìshù zhǎnlǎnguǎn / Dàlián měishùguǎn)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Dalian Art Museum
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A turreted building with tall roofs at the northern end of Victory Bridge, dating from 1902. Sources differ on its first occupant: the Chinese Eastern Railway Company office, Dalny’s Russian administration or, later, a Japanese shipping company. They also disagree on its architect, naming either a German or Skolimowski. It became a nationally protected monument in 2001. A replica stands in the Japanese port of Moji as the Dalian Friendship Memorial. The original now hosts exhibitions.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Victory Bridge
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 胜利桥 (Shènglì qiáo)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A bridge over the railway between Russian Street and the city centre
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A bridge linking the Russian administrative quarter with the rest of Dalny across the railway tracks. Called Nipponbashi under Japanese rule, it became Victory Bridge after 1945. It offers views of the buildings north of the tracks. Sources disagree on the first bridge’s construction and later rebuilding; a Japanese reconstruction in the late 1900s is often mentioned.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: The pedestrian crossing is always open.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Western Park (City Garden?)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 劳动公园 (Láodòng gōngyuán)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Labour Park, the largest park in central Dalian
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: According to Chinese sources, the Russians founded the park in 1898 on what was then the western edge of town and called it Western Park. The Japanese expanded it with sumo, golf and a swimming pool, renaming it Central Park in 1926. It became Lenin Park in 1947 and Labour Park in 1949. The channel has a photograph captioned “City Garden” in Dalny, but whether it shows this park has not been established. Ginkgo trees turn yellow here in autumn.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: Admission is free. The east entrance (劳动公园东门) is a 10–15 minute walk from Zhongshan Square.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Dalny Port (Victoria Bay)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 大连港 (Dàlián gǎng)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Dalian Port, with its passenger terminal (大连港客运站) and Gangwan Square
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: The city was built for this port, designed by Vladimir Sakharov, who had previously built Vladivostok’s commercial harbour. The first phase cost 10.8 million rubles and immediately made Dalny China’s second-busiest cargo port after Shanghai. In May 1904, Japanese troops captured the nearly completed port and used it to supply the army besieging Port Arthur. It remains a major working port; its passenger terminal faces the city. The coordinate marks the terminal.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: The passenger terminal is open to ferry passengers; the cargo port is closed.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Yamato Hotel
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 大连宾馆 (Dàlián bīnguǎn), formerly 大和旅馆
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A hotel on Zhongshan Square
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A South Manchuria Railway hotel opened in 1914 on the south side of Ōhiroba. The railway operated Yamato hotels in the principal cities of Manchuria and Kwantung, including Port Arthur; Dalian’s is the best known. Its colonnaded façade survives and it still operates as a hotel, one of the few pre-war buildings on the square where visitors can stay overnight.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: A working hotel; view its façade from the square.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Yokohama Specie Bank Branch
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 横滨正金银行大连支店旧址 (Héngbīn Zhèngjīn yínháng), now 中国银行
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A Bank of China branch
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A three-domed building from 1909, designed by Tsumaki Yorinaka, a leading Meiji-era Japanese architect, and his pupil Ōta Satoshi. The Yokohama Specie Bank financed foreign trade; Manchurian soybeans and soybean cake passed through Dairen. A Bank of China branch now occupies the building, with a 2005 extension behind it.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: A working bank.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Dairen City Hall
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 大连市役所旧址 (Dàlián shìyìsuǒ), now 中国工商银行
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: An ICBC branch
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: Dairen’s city hall, built in 1919 to a design by Matsumuro Shigemitsu’s team, with a tower above the entrance. It stands on the circular square alongside the 1908 police headquarters, 1920 Bank of Korea, 1917 post office and 1936 Oriental Development Company office. Over thirty years, the Japanese built around the square laid out by the Russians. It now houses ICBC.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: A working bank.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Dairen Police Headquarters
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 大连警察署旧址 (Dàlián jǐngchá shǔ)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: An office building on Zhongshan Square
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: The first building on Ōhiroba, completed in 1908 to a design by Maeda Shōin’s team in the Kwantung Government-General’s construction department. Red brick with white bands and corner towers. In 1908, the Russian square was still an empty circle with radiating streets marked out; this building established the scale and style of what followed. It now houses offices, including a Citibank branch.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: Offices; no public access inside.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Dairen Railway Station
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 大连站 (Dàlián zhàn)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Dalian’s main railway station
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: Opened in 1937, the station separated passenger flows by level: departing passengers ascended ramps to the upper floor, while arrivals left below. Its exterior is often compared with Tokyo’s Ueno Station. Built by the Japanese for the expanding city, it is a different building from Russian Dalny’s station. It remains in use, with a large forecourt.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: An operating station. Metro: Dalian Railway Station.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Russian Cemetery at Goshinji Temple, Nagasaki
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 悟真寺国際墓地 (Japanese: Goshinji kokusai bochi; Chinese: Wùzhēnsì)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Inasa International Cemetery at the Buddhist Goshinji Temple
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: The Russian Pacific Squadron wintered in Nagasaki until 1897, and a Russian sailors’ cemetery grew up at Goshinji Temple in Inasa. The infant Mikhail Mühlberg lies here: born in besieged Port Arthur on 13 November 1904, baptised the day after the surrender, he lived 52 days. Historian Dmitry Nikolayev reconstructed his family’s story from parish registers in “Misha from Nagasaki”, published in Rodina.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: The temple is in Inasa on the western shore of Nagasaki Bay, near Goshinji-mae bus stop (悟真寺前).

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Dalian University of Foreign Languages, Lüshun Campus
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 大连外国语大学（旅顺校区）
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A working university; Russian Club of Dalian excursions meet outside the campus gates
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: Meeting point for the Russian Club of Dalian’s guided Port Arthur excursions, usually around 09:00, with a return transfer here. The campus stands in the new university district east of Lüshun, about 5 km in a straight line from the historic centre and station. The campus itself has no connection with the fortress: it is a convenient meeting point with parking and an address taxis can find. The group continues by car, beginning at Port Arthur station.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: The organisers will specify the exact meeting point at the campus gates and the time; confirm the day before. Search for 大连外国语大学 旅顺校区.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Port Arthur’s Old Town
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 旅顺老城区（黄河路一带）
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Central Lüshun east of Quail Hill, with Russian and Japanese houses beside the Eastern Basin
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: The town beside the Eastern Basin, below Golden and Quail hills, grew up in the days of the Qing fleet. During Russian rule, Pacific Squadron officers and sailors lived here among port offices, shops and restaurants, while the New Town on the western shore was still being built. The Japanese remodelled the centre after 1905, and many buildings visible today are Japanese-era. The map point represents the district, which is best explored on foot.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: Walk from the railway station or the lower Quail Hill cable-car station. Do not photograph military installations beside the harbour. Check locally which buildings are open.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Redoubt No. 1 (East Panlongshan)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 盘龙山东堡垒 (Pánlóngshān dōng bǎolěi)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Remains of a fieldwork in front of the fort line, north of the Great Eagle’s Nest
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: One of two redoubts on Panlongshan, forward of the Eastern Front’s main line between Forts II and III. During the first general assault, 6–11 (19–24) August 1904, the Japanese captured both at great cost, their only gains in that attack. The main line held, and the siege turned to engineering operations. Which redoubt was No. 1 and which No. 2, and what survives, needs checking against the plan and on the ground.
