src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: There is no separate visitor area. The approximate point comes from the 1904 fortress plan. Look for earthwork remains north of Jiguan Shan Road.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Redoubt No. 2 (West Panlongshan)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 盘龙山西堡垒 (Pánlóngshān xī bǎolěi)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Remains of a fieldwork in front of the fort line, east of Erlongshan
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: The second Panlongshan redoubt, west of the first and closer to Fort No. III. Both covered approaches to the Eastern Front’s main line and fell during the August 1904 assault. Japanese trenches then advanced from here towards the main defences. On the 1904 fortress plan, the redoubts already lie behind the Japanese trench line. Their numbering and exact positions need checking against the plan and on site.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: The approximate position comes from the 1904 plan. Any signs are in Chinese only.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Fortification No. 4
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 大案子山堡垒 (Dà Ànzishān bǎolěi)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A fortification on Great Anzishan north of the New Town, marked as a viewpoint on OpenStreetMap
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: An intermediate work on the Western Front between Forts IV and V, directly above the New Town. It is red on the 1904 fortress plan: these positions remained Russian on 19 December. The Japanese did not assault the Western Front, concentrating on 203 Metre Hill and the northeast, and received the work after the surrender. Its design resembles No. 5: rampart, dry ditch and caponiers. The ruins’ condition needs checking on site.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: Approach from the New Town streets (民泰街). Check access and ticket arrangements in advance.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Fort No. IV
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 椅子山堡垒 (Yǐzishān bǎolěi)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A fort on Yizishan northwest of the New Town
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A Western Front fort on Yizishan, or “Chair Hill”, on the northern flank and closest to 203 Metre Hill among this sector’s forts. On the 1904 plan, it remains Russian until the siege ends, like all the western forts: after taking 203 Metre Hill on 22 November (5 December), the Japanese did not advance farther west. The fortress surrendered on 20 December 1904 (2 January 1905), and the fort was occupied without fighting. The OpenStreetMap position agrees with the 1904 plan.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: Approach along Chuncheng Road (春城路). We have no ticket information; check locally.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Battery D
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Site of a permanent battery between Fort No. V and Fortification No. 5
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A permanent Western Front battery. Port Arthur’s land-front batteries were designated by letters. On the 1904 plan, Battery D stands south of Fort V, halfway to Fortification No. 5, covering the valley towards the New Town. The battery took part in artillery action: G. S. Pilsudski’s diary for December 1904 describes its fire and Japanese shelling. Surviving remains and access have not been checked: the point was taken from the plan and may be off by a hundred or two hundred metres.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: An approximate point from the 1904 plan. Compare it with satellite imagery before visiting.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Naval Assembly
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Building not yet identified; the map point is provisional
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: The naval officers’ club, a meeting place and centre of leisure for Pacific Squadron officers in Russian Port Arthur. A Naval Assembly was a regular feature of Russian naval-base life and appears in siege memoirs and diaries. We have not yet identified its building in modern Lüshun or established whether it survives. The point is therefore provisionally placed near Lüshun Museum. We will check the 1904 town plans and the guide’s account.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: Shown on the guided excursion. For independent visits, follow the guide’s description. The map position is provisional.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Yamato Hotel, Lüshun
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 旅顺大和旅馆旧址 (Lǚshùn Dàhé lǚguǎn jiùzhǐ), 文化路30号
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A two-storey mansion of 1903 on Wenhua Road, reported by the press to be in poor condition
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: Distinguish it from Dalian’s Yamato Hotel on Zhongshan Square. The protected-building plaque dates it to 1903. Chinese press reports identify it as the mansion of Ji Fengtai, a Chinese merchant with Russian nationality, converted after the war into a South Manchuria Railway Yamato hotel. The same reports say Puyi stayed here in 1931. In the late 2010s, journalists described cracks in the walls and a construction fence around the house.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: Address: 旅顺口区文化路30号, west of Lüshun Museum. The map point marks the street rather than the house; access inside is unlikely.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Russian School
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Building not yet identified; the map point in the New Town is provisional
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: Officers, officials and employees lived with their families in Russian Port Arthur, and schools opened for their children. We have not yet checked which building is shown as the “Russian School” or its use after 1905. The point is provisionally placed among the New Town’s old streets, where several Japanese-era school buildings survive. We will check town plans and sources before supplying a precise address.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: Shown on the guided excursion. The map position is provisional.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Lüshun’s Japanese Quarters
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 太阳沟历史街区 (中央大街、新华大街一带)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: Taiyanggou streets with administrative buildings and villas from 1905–1945
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: After 1905, the Japanese made Lüshun, or Ryojun, the capital of Kwantung and developed the New Town begun by the Russians. Buildings include the former Kwantung administration, gendarmerie headquarters, the mansion of Manchu Prince Su, who lived here after the Qing fell, schools and Japanese officials’ houses. Many have protected-monument plaques; some are abandoned. The point represents the district, easily explored on foot from the museum.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: Allow 1–1.5 hours to walk from Lüshun Museum along Zhongyang Avenue and Xinhua Avenue. Building plaques are in Chinese.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Red Cross Hospital
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 旅顺红十字医院旧址 (Lǚshùn Hóngshízì yīyuàn jiùzhǐ)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: An old building in the Old Town, in a lane off Huanghe Road, listed as a historic site
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: During the siege of 1904, Red Cross hospitals in Port Arthur employed nurses who had come from Russia. Casualties were so numerous that other buildings were also taken over as wards. This Old Town building is listed as a former Red Cross hospital. Which Russian hospital it housed, and its use under the Japanese, need checking against sources. The point comes from OpenStreetMap.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: In the lane north of Huanghe Road (黄河路北一巷), beside the district hospital. Viewed from outside.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: General Kondratenko’s House
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 康特拉琴柯旧居 (Kāngtèlāqínkē jiùjū)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: A mansion on Ningbo Street in the New Town
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A New Town house presented locally as the residence of Major General Roman Kondratenko, commander of the fortress’s land defences. He was killed at Fort No. II on 2 (15) December 1904, and his remains were taken to St Petersburg in 1905, making this house the routes’ only “peacetime” site associated with him. The attribution comes from a local plaque and map; we have not yet seen documentary confirmation.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: Ningbo Street (宁波街), New Town. Viewed from outside.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Laotieshan Lighthouse
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 老铁山灯塔 (Lǎotiěshān dēngtǎ)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: An operating lighthouse and viewpoint at the southern tip of the Liaodong peninsula
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: The lighthouse stands at Liaodong’s southernmost point, southwest of Lüshun. The notional boundary between the Yellow and Bohai seas runs here; on clear days the viewpoint reveals a band where differently coloured waters meet. The lighthouse was built under the Qing in the late nineteenth century, before the Russians arrived. Check the exact date and equipment’s origins on site. Every ship approaching Port Arthur from the west and Bohai Bay passed this cape, about 13 km in a straight line from the harbour entrance.
src/i18n/en/places.json.visit: About 20 km from central Lüshun, by car or taxi. Travel agencies report paid admission to the viewing area; check hours. The cape is very windy.

src/i18n/en/places.json.name: Great Black Mountain (Dahei Shan)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_zh: 大黑山 (Dàhēishān)
src/i18n/en/places.json.name_now: The highest mountain in Dalian’s six districts, 663 m
src/i18n/en/places.json.summary: A 663 m mountain in Jinzhou district, part of the Qianshan range, with Dalian University’s campus at its foot. It has no direct connection with Port Arthur or Dalny: it is a place for a countryside walk. Rhododendrons and other flowers bloom on the slopes and near the summit in spring.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.title: Port Arthur in a Day
src/i18n/en/routes.json.dek: Car excursion No. 1: the Chinese Eastern Railway station, Baiyushan panorama, Old Town, Russian cemetery, Fort No. 2 and the Great Eagle’s Nest.
src/i18n/en/routes.json.author: Russian Club of Dalian

stops.note: Meet outside the campus and arrange seats in the cars.
The Russian-built station where the Chinese Eastern Railway’s southern branch began. Viewed from outside.
Baiyushan, or Quail Hill, and the tower erected by Tōgō and Nogi to commemorate the capture of the fortress. The best panorama of the harbour.
Central Port Arthur: streets where squadron officers and sailors lived, alongside Japanese-era buildings. Lunch in a café afterwards.
The Russian military cemetery, burial place of the fortress’s defenders.
Fort No. 2, where General Kondratenko was killed on 2 (15) December 1904.
The final stop: one of the last heights to fall before the surrender. Transfer back to the university afterwards, provisionally.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.practical: A guided excursion devised by the Russian Club of Dalian; timings at each stop are approximate. Meet around 09:00 at the foreign languages university campus in Lüshun, with a return transfer to the same place. Travel between stops is by car. Baiyushan and the forts are windy; wear comfortable footwear for Fort No. 2 and the Eagle’s Nest. Dongjiguanshan, which includes Fort No. 2, charges admission; check opening hours. Do not photograph military sites by the harbour. Confirm dates, prices and group arrangements with the organisers.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.title: The Eastern Front
src/i18n/en/routes.json.dek: Fort No. 2, the Great Eagle’s Nest, Fort No. 3, the Panlongshan redoubts and Fortification No. 3: eastern-front positions that fell in 1904.
src/i18n/en/routes.json.author: Russian Club of Dalian

stops.note: The fort’s casemates and the stone marking Kondratenko’s death. Begin at the museum by the entrance.
The height fell on 19 December 1904 (1 January 1905). It overlooks the whole Eastern Front.
The fort on Erlongshan, captured on 15 (28) December after its parapet was blown up.
The Panlongshan redoubts fell during the August 1904 assault. Locations are approximate, taken from the 1904 plan.
The second redoubt, farther west. Check the plan: not every site has a sign.
The work on Songshushan, blown up by a Japanese mine on 18 (31) December 1904. The crater remains visible.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.practical: The sites are close together, but hills and few paths make a car more convenient. Before visiting, read the channel’s explanation of a fort’s ditch, escarp, caponier and postern. Late autumn or early spring offers the clearest view of the terrain, without foliage. Bring a torch for the posterns. Redoubt coordinates are approximate and need checking on the ground.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.title: The Western Front
src/i18n/en/routes.json.dek: Fortification No. 5, Battery D, Fortification No. 4 and Fort No. 4: a route along the fortress’s western line.
src/i18n/en/routes.json.author: Russian Club of Dalian

stops.note: The fortress’s best-preserved defensive work: ditch, caponiers, posterns and a small museum room with a model.
A lettered battery between Fortification No. 5 and Fort No. V. Its approximate position is taken from the 1904 plan.
The fortification on Great Anzishan, above the New Town.
The fort on Yizishan, on the northern flank of the Western Front. There is a view of 203 Metre Hill.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.practical: The Western Front receives few visitors and has little signage: save the coordinates in advance. Fortification No. 5 stands in woodland; use 38.7970, 121.1933 for navigation. Battery D’s position comes from the 1904 plan; compare it with satellite imagery. The route combines easily with nearby 203 Metre Hill.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.title: A Walk through Lüshun
src/i18n/en/routes.json.dek: The station, Baiyushan, the New Town’s Japanese quarters, the Old Town and General Kondratenko’s house.
src/i18n/en/routes.json.author: Russian Club of Dalian

stops.note: The terminus of the Chinese Eastern Railway’s southern branch. The walk begins here.
Climb Baiyushan, or Quail Hill, for the tower and harbour panorama.
Lüshun Museum and the square in front, at the beginning of the New Town.
The Naval Assembly, the squadron officers’ club. A guide will identify the building; its map position is provisional.
The Lüshun Yamato Hotel, a former mansion built in 1903. Distinguish it from the Dalian hotel.
The Russian school. The map position is provisional; a guide will identify the building.
The New Town’s Japanese quarters: Kwantung administration buildings, gendarmerie and villas.
The former Red Cross hospital in the Old Town, best reached by taxi.
The final stop: General Kondratenko’s house in the New Town.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.practical: A walking route with short taxi journeys: the harbour and Quail Hill separate the New and Old Towns, about 3 km apart. Baiyushan can be climbed by road or reached by cable car from the station. The Naval Assembly and Russian school are provisionally marked on the map; a guide will show the buildings. Many houses can only be viewed from outside. Stop timings are approximate.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.title: Baiyushan and the Lighthouse
src/i18n/en/routes.json.dek: Quail Hill, Lüshun Prison, the historic centre, the Russian cemetery and Laotieshan Lighthouse where two seas meet.
src/i18n/en/routes.json.author: Russian Club of Dalian

stops.note: Baiyushan: the tower and views of the harbour, Golden Hill and Tiger’s Tail.
Lüshun Prison: grey brick marks the Russian building, red brick the Japanese blocks.
A walk through Lüshun’s historic centre along the New Town streets.
The Russian military cemetery, where the fortress’s defenders are buried.
The lighthouse on Cape Laotieshan, where the Yellow and Bohai seas meet.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.practical: A car is needed between stops: Laotieshan Lighthouse is about 20 km from central Lüshun. Travel agencies report that the prison closes on Mondays, so choose another day. Lighthouse admission is paid; check opening hours. The cape and Baiyushan are windy. Stop timings are approximate.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.title: Russian Dalny on Foot
src/i18n/en/routes.json.dek: From Skolimowski’s circular square, across the bridge to Dalny’s first district and Sakharov’s port.

stops.note: Stand at the centre and find the ten radiating streets: the 1899 plan remains legible on the ground. The surrounding buildings are Japanese-era.
The bridge over the railway separated the Russian administrative quarter from the rest of the city. It offers views of the buildings on the north side.
A Russian building from 1902. Look at its turrets and roofs, then visit the exhibition if it is open.
Formerly Inzhenernaya Street. Distinguish original buildings from replicas by their masonry and window proportions.
The city administration building at the end of the street, from which Sakharov governed Dalny.
The port for which the city was built. Victoria Bay’s quays can be seen from the passenger terminal.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.practical: The most convenient start is Zhongshan Square metro station. Russian Street is about a kilometre away on foot across Victory Bridge. The roughly 2 km stretch from Russian Street to the port is less rewarding as a walk and can be covered by taxi. Russian Street has many souvenir shops; original buildings are concentrated near its northern end and around the administration building. Traffic around the square is busy: use the underpasses. May, when black locust trees flower, and September–October are the best months.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.title: Japanese Dairen
src/i18n/en/routes.json.dek: The city of 1905–1945, built on the Russian plan: the station, banks on Ōhiroba Square, the Yamato Hotel and the port.

stops.note: The 1937 station, designed to separate passenger flows by floor.
The square’s first building, dating from 1908.
The Yokohama Specie Bank’s three domes, 1909.
Walk around the circle: the 1917 post office, the 1920 Bank of Korea and the 1936 Oriental Development Company building.
The 1919 city hall with its corner tower.
The South Manchuria Railway’s hotel, opened in 1914 and still operating.
The port for which Japan held Kwantung for forty years.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.practical: The station is about a kilometre from Zhongshan Square along Zhongshan Road. The buildings on the square are working banks: you can enter during business hours, but photography in banking halls is usually prohibited. The façades are illuminated at night, making this a possible dusk walk. Luxun Road (鲁迅路) leads towards the port and still has pre-war buildings. If you have energy left, add Labour Park, the Japanese-era Central Park.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.title: Lüshun Cherry Blossom
src/i18n/en/routes.json.dek: A seasonal route for the second half of April: Longwangtang Reservoir’s garden, the garden at 203 Metre Hill and the view from Quail Hill.

stops.note: The best-known cherry garden near Dalian. Single-flowered varieties bloom around mid-April; double-flowered varieties follow a week later.
The garden at the foot of the hill flowers roughly a week later than Longwangtang. Climb to the summit monument.
Lunch and a walk in the New Town.
Sunset over the harbour.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.practical: Flowering dates shift each year. Tourism reports for 2026 placed the start at Longwangtang around 14–15 April and the peak around 19–28 April; 203 Metre Hill followed a week later, into early May. Peak weekends bring traffic and queues; weekdays are noticeably quieter. Longwangtang admission cost 20 yuan in 2025; seasonal prices at 203 Metre Hill may differ. Excursion buses run from Dalian during blossom season. If the blossom has finished, the route also works in May, when black locust trees flower in the New Town.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.title: Zhongshan in an hour
src/i18n/en/routes.json.dek: A circular square, the Yamato Hotel and Yokohama Specie Bank: a short self-guided walk in central Dalian, with all three stops viewed from outside.

stops.note: Begin with the shape of the square: the circle and streets radiating from it. The layout comes from Russian Dalny; the hotel and bank ahead belong to Japanese Dairen.
Find the arched canopy above the entrance, then follow the rhythm of columns across the façade. The former Yamato Hotel, now 大连宾馆, was completed in 1914.
Look up at the three domes and compare the bank’s strict symmetry with the hotel’s longer façade. This is the former Yokohama Specie Bank, built in 1909.

src/i18n/en/routes.json.practical: A self-guided walk viewing buildings from outside. Start at 中山广场 and finish at 中国银行大连市分行, 中山广场9号. Allow about an hour for walking, crossings and three stops. The Amap walking link leads to the next stop; if the app changes mode, select “步行” (walking). Use marked crossings.

src/i18n/en/series.json.title: The Russo-Japanese War in Five Posts
A Photographic Chronicle of the War
The Architects of Far Eastern Policy

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: The Mokshan Regiment on the Hills of Manchuria: Waltz
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: Ilya Shatrov
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: The bandmaster of the 214th Mokshan Regiment led his musicians onto the parapet near Mukden as the regiment fought its way out of encirclement; seven of the 61 musicians survived. A year later he wrote a waltz in memory of his comrades. Initially received coolly, its score was then reprinted 82 times in three years. The post links to a recording with lyrics.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: The Russo-Japanese War, 1904–1905: A Lecture by Kirill Nazarenko
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: Kirill Nazarenko
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: A lecture by a naval historian and St Petersburg State University professor, delivered at the Museum of Political History of Russia and published by Digital History. In 1 hour 20 minutes it moves from the causes of the war to its remembrance: Kwantung, the “Bezobrazov clique”, the night attack, Varyag and Steregushchy, the Yellow Sea battle and the surrender. Sober without being dismissive, it also supplies the idea of hindsight explored in a separate channel post.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: MINAEV LIVE: The Russo-Japanese War
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: Sergei Minayev
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: An hour-long episode on the empire before the war, Port Arthur, Mukden, Tsushima, Portsmouth and the reasons for Russia’s defeat. Historians prepared the material; the presenter, trained as a historian and archivist, tells it with energy and feeling. The channel particularly recommends it for anyone wanting to understand the war in one evening, though the advertising requires patience.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: The Russo-Japanese War, 1904–1905: Album, Commander-in-Chief’s Headquarters, 1905
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: Published by the Commander-in-Chief’s Headquarters; printed by S. M. Prokudin-Gorsky
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: Around 300 plates of front-line photographs, persistently attributed to Prokudin-Gorsky although he only compiled and printed the album. It offers a view from the Manchurian army’s headquarters: the Shahe and Putilov Hill with a Shimose shell bursting, trenches and shelters made of sorghum, Chinese New Year and, unexpectedly for an official publication, the retreat from Mukden to Tieling. All the plates can be browsed online.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: Album of the Wartime Life of the XVII Army Corps during the Russo-Japanese War, 1904–1905
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: Corps of Military Topographers
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: A second war album associated with Prokudin-Gorsky: 54 plates and 231 photographic reproductions. His workshops made the blocks and printed it; the Corps of Military Topographers compiled and published it. It does not show his personal photographic view of the war, but does demonstrate the quality of his printing. Individual plates are available in the State Historical Museum’s online catalogue.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: Manchuria: An Illustrated Album of the Russo-Japanese War
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: A. V. Martynov, editor and publisher
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: An album of 122 plates published in St Petersburg in 1906, just after Portsmouth, by R. Golike and A. Wilborg. It presents a contemporary view while the war was still raw, showing how people wanted it remembered. Digitised by the State Public Historical Library and freely available on Internet Archive without registration.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: Nichiro Sen’eki Shashinchō (日露戦役寫眞帖): A Photographic Album of the Russo-Japanese War
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: A Japanese photographic album held by the National Diet Library in Tokyo. A view from the other side of the parapet: photographs illustrate the post on relieving boredom in the positions around Port Arthur, including applause from enemy trenches and “Port Arthur roulette”.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: S. M. Prokudin-Gorsky’s Colour Photographs at the Library of Congress
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: Sergei Prokudin-Gorsky
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: More than 2,600 colour photographs from 1905–1915, acquired from the photographer’s sons by the US Library of Congress in 1948 and now freely available. Prokudin-Gorsky did not photograph the Russo-Japanese War, a persistent legend examined separately by the channel, but the collection offers valuable views of the period.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: Russian Archives Electronic Reading Room: Finding Aids for RGVIA Collection 487
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: Rosarkhiv
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: The channel suggests beginning archival research here. The electronic reading room provides finding aids for Collection 487 of the Russian State Military Historical Archive, “The Russo-Japanese War, 1904–1905”: almost 1,500 files, from General Sakharov’s reports to Nicholas II to defender Kvatu’s memoir The Truth about Port Arthur. The same archive holds Kuropatkin’s personal papers and records of the Manchurian army’s rear services.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: A Guide to Russian Archives on the Russo-Japanese War
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: A guide to what is held where: naval records in the Russian State Naval Archive, including Aurora officers’ reports on Tsushima; photographs in the Russian State Documentary Film and Photo Archive; the proposed General Commissariat in Manchuria in the State Archive of the Russian Federation; diplomacy in the Archive of Foreign Policy of the Russian Empire; and the home front in the Russian State Historical Archive of the Far East. Archives have also published document collections on Port Arthur’s defence. Much remains in descendants’ family collections.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: Japan Center for Asian Historical Records (JACAR)
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: National Archives of Japan
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: A Japanese centre digitising documents from three institutions: the National Archives, the Foreign Ministry’s Diplomatic Archives and the National Institute for Defense Studies. Material includes the imperial declaration of war, Portsmouth conference records and the Nichiro Sen’eki series of operational reports, divisional journals and casualty statistics. The interface is in English and Japanese.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: National Electronic Library (Russia)
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: A resource the channel’s author recommends for finding and reading pre-revolutionary books and later publications. Among its holdings is Kotwicz and Borodovsky’s 1898 booklet Liaodong and Its Ports, describing Dalian Bay a year before Dalny’s foundation.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: A Comic Based on the Channel’s First Posts
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: The channel author’s husband
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: A graphic version of the opening posts, “How It All Began”, “Russia Goes East” and “Korea, Manchuria and the Timber Concessions”: from the Meiji Restoration and Sino-Japanese War to Russian concessions in Korea.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: Video: How Fortification No. 5 Worked
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: The channel author’s husband
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: A reconstruction based on the channel’s post about Fortification No. 5 on Port Arthur’s western flank, one of the few land-front works completed before the war. The channel reports no separate assault, but G. S. Pilsudski’s diary records the work’s artillery service. The video shows the ditch, caponiers, casemates and parapet described in the text.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: The Russo-Japanese War on Neolurk
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: The internet’s account of the war, for adults: its structure is as clear as a textbook, from the night attack to Portsmouth, but its vocabulary is very different. It reads in one sitting, makes Kuropatkin and Stessel unforgettable and gives Rozhestvensky’s justifications their own section. Entertainment rather than a source: some figures are bolder than the Japanese infantry. The channel’s advice is Neolurk for the mood, then Martin for the conscience.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: Leo Tolstoy: Bethink Yourselves! (1904)
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: Leo Tolstoy
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: Written by the 75-year-old Tolstoy amid the patriotic enthusiasm of early 1904, the essay was rejected by every Russian newspaper. It failed to stop the war but outlived both war and censorship. Tolstoy writes about the enthusiasm of people who will not fight themselves and asks who wages war if every individual opposes it.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: Misha from Nagasaki: An Article in Rodina
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: Dmitry Nikolayev
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: The smallest child of Port Arthur: Mikhail Mühlberg was born in the besieged fortress on 13 November 1904, baptised the day after the surrender, lived 52 days and was buried in the Russian cemetery at Goshinji Temple in Nagasaki. Using parish registers and archives, the historian reconstructed the lives of his family: a wounded father decorated with the Order of St George and a grandmother who worked in a hospital throughout the siege.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: Port Arthur: Unexpected Findings from Literary and Archival Research
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: D. K. Nikolayev, O. V. Chistyakov
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: An article in the Military Historical Journal, 2010, No. 1, that failed to substantiate the legend of Port Arthur’s author: archival records showed that neither Alexander Stepanov nor his father had defended the fortress or visited the city. Another life emerged instead, that of a Guards artilleryman in the First World War, about which the writer remained silent throughout his life.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: Konstantin Balmont: Our Tsar (1906)
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: Konstantin Balmont
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: Opening with “Our tsar is Mukden, our tsar is Tsushima”, the poem is still quoted as a brief verdict on the war. It cost the poet years abroad: he could return only under the 1913 amnesty marking the Romanov tercentenary. The post includes the full text.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: “It Was Horrific”: Khodynka, 1896
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: Artyom Lokalov
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: A Rodina article on the crush at Khodynka Field during Nicholas II’s coronation celebrations. The channel offers it as further reading for its post on the tragedy and the Russian-Chinese treaty of 1896. Published on 30 May 2026.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: Rodina: The Later Lives of the Imperial Family’s Executioners
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: Rodina magazine
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: An article dated 17 July 2018 about what happened to participants in the execution. Linked from the post on the Ipatiev House, Nicholas II and Dr Botkin.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: Zodchiy, 1904: On Designing the Plan of the City of Dalny
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: Kazimierz Skolimowski
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: Skolimowski's paper appeared in issues 12–14 of 1904. S. S. Levoshko's bibliography gives pp. 141–144, 153–155 and 161–166 respectively; the original pages have not been checked here. The channel post includes plans and photographs. The link leads to a mirror of the annual volume, not the publisher's archive.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: The Defence of Port Arthur, 1904–1905: Doctors and Nurses
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: P. V. Mandryka Central Military Clinical Hospital
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: Medical care in the besieged fortress: surgeon Viktor von Hübbenet’s work, shortages of staff and dressings, the hospital ship Mongolia and nurse Wilhelmina Krieg’s assistance on 203 Metre Hill.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: Ship Logistics During the Russo-Japanese War: Rice Balls Were Served for a Post-Victory Dinner
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: Akinori Ishihara (石原明徳)
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: A study from Japan’s National Institute for Defense Studies, published as NIDS Commentary No. 324 on 28 May 2024. Pages 7–8 discuss supply ships, Mikasa’s menu for 30 May 1904 and cases of food poisoning. This is a modern work based on naval documents; the original medical volume has not been checked separately.

src/i18n/en/sources.json.title: Finance in Colonial Dalian under Japanese Rule
src/i18n/en/sources.json.author: Sun Yaoting (孙耀庭)
src/i18n/en/sources.json.annotation: A bank clerk’s later memoir in the second issue of Materials on the History of Dalian. The issue’s publication date has not been established. On the checked pages, 49–53 of the library PDF, the author recalls entering banking in 1930 and describes currency circulation and access to credit. The article continues beyond this extract; the full text has not been checked. Digitised by Dalian Municipal Library.

spring.title: Cherry blossom at Longwangtang
spring.note: Single-flowered varieties bloom around mid-April; double-flowered varieties follow roughly a week later.

spring.title: Cherry blossom at 203 Metre Hill
spring.note: The garden at the foot of 203 Metre Hill blooms about a week later than Longwangtang.

spring.title: Spring flowers on Dahei Shan
spring.note: Rhododendrons flower near the summit, with other spring flowers on the slopes. The ridge is often windy, so choose a calm day.

spring.title: Dalian Acacia Festival
spring.note: The black locust blossom festival has been held since 1990; in 2011 it ran from 25 to 31 May. Venues change from year to year.

spring.title: Blossom in the New Town
spring.note: Black locust trees line the streets of Taiyanggou in Lüshun.

spring.title: The forts before the leaves return
spring.note: Before the trees leaf out, the fortifications’ ditches and earthworks are easiest to see.

summer.title: Sweet cherries in Lüshun
summer.when: early June; from late May in warm years
summer.note: Since 2009, the district has held the title of China’s home of large sweet cherries. Trees grown outdoors flower in mid-April, and the fruit ripens 42 days later.

summer.title: Swimming season
summer.note: Some beaches remain closed in mid-July. In August 2026, water temperatures ranged from 24–30 °C in bulletins from China’s Ministry of Ecology and Environment.

summer.title: The sea below Golden Hill
summer.note: Lüshun’s town beach lies at the foot of the hill, beside Electric Cliff Battery.

summer.title: Shade at Fortification No. 5
summer.note: The fortification stands in woodland, cooler in hot weather than the exposed hills.

summer.title: Dalian’s port and waterfront
summer.note: Gangwan Square and the passenger terminal offer convenient views of the port.

autumn.title: The fishing season opens
autumn.note: The fishing ban in the Yellow and Bohai seas runs from 1 May until 12:00 on 1 September. Dalian marks its end with celebrations as boats leave the ports.

autumn.title: Ginkgo trees in Labour Park
autumn.note: The park is described as one of Dalian’s best places to see golden ginkgo leaves.

autumn.title: The land front on a clear day
autumn.note: The weather is dry, the leaves are falling, and the heights offer views along the whole line of hills.

autumn.title: The view from Quail Hill
autumn.note: In autumn, views across the harbour and hills reach farther than in the humid summer.

winter.title: The Russian cemetery in winter
winter.note: Visitors bring flowers on anniversaries of the defence; there are few people.

winter.title: 5 December: the loss of 203 Metre Hill
winter.note: On this day in 1904, Russian troops abandoned 203 Metre Hill, giving the enemy a view into the harbour.

winter.title: 15 December: Kondratenko’s death
winter.note: A stone at Fort No. II marks the place where the general was killed.

winter.title: 2 January: the fortress surrenders
winter.note: The surrender was signed on 20 December 1904 (2 January 1905). Stessel met Nogi at Shuishiying on 23 December (5 January).

winter.title: 9 February: the war begins
winter.note: Japanese destroyers attacked the squadron off Port Arthur at night. Quail Hill offers the best view of the harbour.

books_unmatched.hodyakov-zheltorossiya: M. V. Khodyakov. “Yellow Russia” in the Geopolitical Plans of the Russian Military Elite in the Late Nineteenth and Early Twentieth Centuries (2018)
books_unmatched.lenin-padenie-port-artura: V. I. Lenin. The Fall of Port Arthur

people.abaza: Rear admiral, cousin and political ally of Alexander Bezobrazov. He belonged to the circle of Yalu timber-concession shareholders. The venture began commercially, but building fortifications under cover of logging tied it to Russia’s advance in Korea and pre-war rivalry with Japan.
people.aleksandr-iii: Emperor of Russia and father of Nicholas II. Sergei Witte’s rise and Russia’s rapprochement with France began under him. In 1891 Alexander III listened to the Marseillaise at Kronstadt, a striking moment in an autocratic empire’s alliance with a republic. French loans later helped finance Russia’s railway projects.
people.barabash: Russian general who proposed in 1887 that, in a war with China, forces should concentrate on Manchuria and, if unsuccessful, advance on Beijing. His memorandum appears in a study of “Yellow Russia” projects. It illustrates a military route to expanding Russian influence discussed before the Kwantung lease.
people.bezobrazov-pyotr: Vice admiral who temporarily commanded the Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment. Under him, the detachment attacked Japanese transports in the Korea Strait in June 1904. He should not be confused with Alexander Mikhailovich Bezobrazov, the court-connected entrepreneur involved in the Yalu concession.
people.borodovskii: Orientalist who wrote Liaodong and Its Ports: Port Arthur and Dalianwan with Władysław Kotwicz. Published in St Petersburg in summer 1898, shortly after the Russian lease began, the 47-page booklet described the peninsula and its ports before Russian Dalny was built.
people.briner: Vladivostok merchant who obtained a Korean timber concession on the Yalu and Tumen rivers in 1896. It was later acquired by participants in the venture associated with Alexander Bezobrazov. Briner’s name marks the original business deal from which a political project developed.
people.chertkov: Publisher and friend of Leo Tolstoy. He helped publish the anti-war essay Bethink Yourselves! abroad after Russian newspapers rejected it. Chertkov sent the text to England, where it appeared in The Times in summer 1904. Tolstoy’s appeal to his contemporaries thus found readers beyond the Russian press.
people.denikin: Russian officer who sharply criticised Russia’s Far Eastern policy in 1908. He considered the Chinese Eastern Railway’s economic value small and its long route across foreign territory strategically disadvantageous; he called the troop presence in Manchuria an occupation. He chiefly blamed Witte. This judgment was made after defeat in the war.
people.dubasov: Russian admiral involved in the occupation of Kwantung. The overview of the two cities names him among the earliest leaders of Russia’s presence on the peninsula, before Subotich and Alekseyev. His name belongs to the opening chapter of Russian Port Arthur and Dalny.
people.essen: Naval officer who commanded the battleship Sevastopol during the final phase of Port Arthur’s defence. When siege artillery began shelling the ships in the inner harbour, he moved the battleship to White Wolf Bay. After repelling destroyer attacks, her crew scuttled her before the fortress surrendered.
people.georg-grecheskii: Greek prince and cousin of the future Nicholas II. He joined the Eastern journey at Piraeus and accompanied the heir in Japan. He should not be confused with Nicholas’s younger brother, Georgy Alexandrovich, who also began the journey but fell ill and returned home.
people.grodekov: Governor-General of the Amur region and a participant in debates over Manchuria’s future. In the memorandum quoted by the channel, he opposed both abandoning influence there and outright annexation. After the Russo-Japanese War, he warned of another possible conflict with Japan.
people.hodyakov: Historian who examined plans for Russian policy in Manchuria through military memoranda in the archives. His study of “Yellow Russia” underpins a channel article. It shows that advocates of annexation had no shared idea of how the territory would be governed.
people.ivanov-13: Lieutenant aboard Rurik who took command after the captain and senior officers died fighting Japanese cruisers. With her steering disabled, the ship could no longer escape. Ivanov ordered her scuttled to keep her from the enemy; the Japanese rescued surviving sailors. Ivanov the Thirteenth later became a rear admiral.
people.kirill-vladimirovich: Grand duke and cousin of Nicholas II. The Port Arthur overview connects him with the beginning of the Russian lease: on 16 (28) March 1898 he raised the Russian flag over Golden Hill. Russia and China had signed the convention leasing Liaodong’s southern tip the previous day.
people.kokovtsov: Russian finance minister, later chairman of the Council of Ministers. The account of Nicholas II compares his memoirs with Witte’s judgments. Kokovtsov portrayed the emperor as a decent man too susceptible to his entourage. This is testimony about the ruler’s character, rather than a complete explanation of the war’s causes.
people.kolchak: Naval officer and defender of Port Arthur. During the Russo-Japanese War he commanded the destroyer Serdity; his service aboard Diana in Stepanov’s novel is a fictional departure. Alexander Lysev used his notebook in researching the fortress’s everyday life.
people.kotvich: Orientalist who prepared the 1898 booklet Liaodong and Its Ports: Port Arthur and Dalianwan with Leonid Borodovsky. They described the newly leased territory, its geography and ports. The publication allows comparison between early impressions of Liaodong and what was subsequently built at Dalny and Port Arthur.
people.kulichkin: Author of a biography of Roman Kondratenko in the Lives of Remarkable People series, as well as historical fiction about Port Arthur. The channel reviews his book as a military biography with strong judgments about the general and his colleagues. The review helps separate the events from the author’s interpretation.
people.lenin: Bolshevik leader and author of The Fall of Port Arthur. He viewed the fortress’s surrender in relation to the political crisis of the autocracy. The channel compares this perspective with later Soviet accounts and changing interpretations of Russia’s defeat.
people.levitov: Journalist and ethnographer associated on the channel with the idea of “Yellow Russia”. He proposed a buffer colony between Lake Baikal and the Pacific, outlining it in a 1905 report. This was a project of its time, rather than the name of an administrative territory that actually existed.
people.linevich: Russian general who commanded a force in the allied advance on Beijing during the Boxer Rebellion. The channel notes that it was drawn mainly from the Kwantung garrison. His involvement connects the events of 1900 in northern China with Russia’s presence at Port Arthur.
people.lysev: Author of Russian Port Arthur in 1904: A History of Everyday Military Life. He studied food, housing, supplies and leisure among the garrison and civilians. Official returns and administrative records are compared with diaries and memoirs, revealing how the fortress lived between battles.
people.martin-kristofer: British author of an overview of the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905. The channel suggests it as one way into the subject. Its review weighs the strengths of a coherent narrative against the limitations of a book written long before current research.
people.meidzi: Japanese emperor during Nicholas’s Eastern journey and the Russo-Japanese War. In the account of Ōtsu, he personally helped resolve the crisis after the attack on the Russian heir. Meiji is also used as an era name in Japanese publications and catalogues.
people.minaev: Author and presenter of MINAEV LIVE. His hour-long Russo-Japanese War episode moves from imperial pre-war policy through Port Arthur, Mukden and Tsushima to Portsmouth. The channel recommends it as a modern popular introduction; the site’s library preserves the video link.
people.molodyakov: Historian of Japan and author of studies of international relations and culture. The channel reviews his books on the Franco-Russian alliance and Russia’s rapprochement with Japan after the war. They connect Port Arthur’s history with diplomacy, loans and changing relations between former enemies.
people.myulberg-evgenii: Second lieutenant and defender of Port Arthur, father of the infant Mikhail Mühlberg. According to Dmitry Nikolayev’s archival research, discussed on the channel, he was wounded and awarded the Order of St George. The family’s story was reconstructed through documents and the child’s grave in Nagasaki’s Russian cemetery.
people.nazarenko: Naval historian whose lecture on the Russo-Japanese War is recommended by the channel. A central theme is hindsight: judging decisions made by people who did not yet know how the war would end. The lecture helps readers approach the defence without assuming defeat was obvious to everyone involved.
people.nikolaev-dk: Historian who reconstructs individual lives from archival documents. Using parish registers, he studied the family of the infant Mikhail Mühlberg, buried in Nagasaki. With Oleg Chistyakov, he checked the claim that Alexander Stepanov and his father had defended Port Arthur: archival research did not confirm their presence in the fortress.
people.panishchev: Author of The Crisis of Moral Consciousness in Russia and the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905. The channel reviews it critically, examining how moral explanations of defeat relate to specific military events. This entry leads to that review; its judgments are those of the channel’s author.
people.poselyagin: Writer of the alternative-history series The Twins, including Ensigns of the Admiralty and Lieutenants of the Admiralty. The books are set around Port Arthur and the Russo-Japanese War. The channel discusses them as fiction that changes events and the lives of historical figures.
people.reitsenshtein: Naval officer who temporarily led the Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment before Karl Jessen’s appointment. He appears in the history of its operations and in the review of Valentin Pikul’s Cruisers. These articles allow readers to compare the historical participant with his fictional portrayal.
people.rennenkampf: Russian general commanding a mounted force in Manchuria. The 1905 land-war album includes photographs of his Transbaikal Cossacks and the commander-in-chief’s visit. They show the Manchurian army in another theatre of war, far from besieged Port Arthur.
people.rozhestvenskii: Admiral who commanded the Second Pacific Squadron on its voyage to the Far East, ending at the Battle of Tsushima. The channel discusses him in its overview of the war and its review of an online account examining command decisions and later explanations of defeat.
people.ruzvelt: US president who mediated the end of the Russo-Japanese War. His involvement helped bring about the Portsmouth negotiations in 1905. The channel connects Roosevelt’s diplomatic role with Witte’s actions, Japan’s demands and the peace terms.
people.saginadze: Historian and author of A Reformer after the Reforms: S. Yu. Witte and Russian Society, 1906–1915. Her research underpins the article on Witte’s reputation after his retirement. It examines newspapers, satire, public expectations and political struggles conducted through the press.
people.shevchenko-av: Compiler of Anecdotes of the Russian Empire: The Russo-Japanese War, reviewed on the channel. The collection offers material on reputations and ways of making sense of the war. A joke conveys the attitudes of its teller and audience; by itself, it does not establish that an event occurred.
people.skitalets: Pen name of Stepan Petrov. The channel names him as the author of an early set of lyrics for Ilya Shatrov’s waltz On the Hills of Manchuria. The music was originally instrumental; its lyrics and their later variations form a separate history of its reception.
people.smirnov: Commandant of Port Arthur during the siege. This post should be distinguished from command of the Kwantung Fortified Region, held by Stessel, and the land defences, led by Kondratenko. The channel also discusses Smirnov’s dispute with Alexander Fok and their duel in 1908.
people.sozonov: Participant in the 1904 assassination of Interior Minister Vyacheslav von Plehve. The channel uses this episode to close its account of the minister and the remark about a “small victorious war” attributed to him. Sozonov’s later life involved penal servitude and protest against the punishment of political prisoners.
people.stalin: Soviet leader. The articles on remembrance compare the Bolshevik attitude towards the autocracy’s defeat with his 1945 speech after victory over Japan. This shows how the same historical event acquired different meanings in the political language of different years.
people.stark: Vice admiral commanding the Port Arthur squadron when war began. During the night of 27 January (9 February) 1904, Japanese destroyers attacked the outer roadstead, damaging Retvizan, Tsesarevich and Pallada. Commanders changed over the squadron’s subsequent history; this opening blow fell during Stark’s tenure.
people.suvorin: Publisher of Novoye Vremya. He recruited Mikhail Menshikov, whose Letters to My Neighbours appeared several times a week, and corresponded with Sergei Witte. His newspaper shows how debate about the war and ministers became part of the struggle for public opinion.
people.takahasi: Japanese financier and statesman. During the Russo-Japanese War, he helped secure foreign loans, including in London and New York. The channel connects his work with the question of why military victories did not spare Japan financial exhaustion or the need for peace.
people.togo: Japanese admiral who commanded the fleet in the Russo-Japanese War. The channel’s overview follows the naval campaign from the attacks off Port Arthur to Tsushima. His name connects fleet operations across battles often read as separate episodes.
people.trusov: Captain of the Vladivostok detachment’s cruiser Rurik. He was killed in action against Japanese cruisers; after the senior officers died, Konstantin Ivanov took command. Trusov also appears in Pikul’s Cruisers, the subject of a separate channel review.
people.tsuda-sandzo: Japanese policeman who attacked the Russian heir Nicholas with a sabre at Ōtsu in 1891. The attack cut short the Japanese leg of his Eastern journey and caused a diplomatic crisis. The channel treats it as an episode in the future emperor’s life, separately from the causes of the 1904 war.
people.tsysi: Qing empress dowager who influenced Chinese policy in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. She appears in the channel’s biography of Li Hongzhang and its account of the Boxer Rebellion. These articles explain the Chinese court’s position under pressure from foreign powers.
people.uhtomskii: Rear admiral who took command after Wilhelm Vitgeft died in the Yellow Sea battle. The principal Russian ships returned to Port Arthur, while others went to neutral ports and were disarmed. Command within the fortress later passed to Robert Viren.
people.viren: Rear admiral who succeeded Ukhtomsky in command of Port Arthur’s naval forces. In the final phase, guns were removed from ships for the forts and sailors went to land positions. After 203 Metre Hill was lost, ships remaining in the harbour came under accurately directed siege-artillery fire.
people.yaroslavskii: Bolshevik journalist and party historian who wrote a booklet on the Russo-Japanese War. The channel treats it as an example of Soviet explanations of the war through the Revolution of 1905. In this reading, military defeats mattered above all for their effect on the autocracy.
people.ayrapetov: Historian and author of On the Road to Collapse: The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905. The book connects military operations with diplomacy, finance and decisions in St Petersburg. The channel recommends it as a study of the whole war, grounded in documents, memoirs and correspondence.
people.akunin: Author of The Diamond Chariot, a novel about Erast Fandorin. Its two settings, Japan in 1878 and wartime Russia in 1905, are joined by a detective plot. The channel suggests it as a fictional introduction while maintaining the distinction between invention and the documentary history of intelligence.
people.gyubbenet: Chief surgeon of the Port Arthur fortress, whose work is described in the article on medical care during the siege. The channel highlights operations for abdominal wounds and the conditions in which casualties were treated. His name also appears in discussions of different ways to count garrison losses.
people.krig: Volunteer nurse who cared for the wounded during the defence of Port Arthur. According to the medical article retold on the channel, she reached a dressing station under fire during the fighting for 203 Metre Hill and received the Medal for Bravery. The episode forms part of the fortress’s medical history.
people.krivosheev: Editor of the statistical study Russia and the USSR in the Wars of the Twentieth Century, used in the article on the cost of defending Port Arthur. It compares troop strength, armaments, casualties and prisoners. The book’s different accounting categories cannot be combined into a single death toll.
people.gilyarovsky: Writer, reporter and witness to the Khodynka disaster. His account is used in the channel article on Nicholas II’s coronation. It places the Moscow events of 1896 alongside Li Hongzhang’s visit and the negotiations that opened the way for the Chinese Eastern Railway.
people.yurovsky: Commandant of the Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, tasked with carrying out the decision to execute the imperial family and their companions. Among the dead was Yevgeny Botkin, a doctor and veteran of the Russo-Japanese War. The channel explicitly notes uncertainty over the exact membership of the execution squad.
people.beloborodov: Chairman of the Ural Regional Soviet in 1918. The channel identifies its presidium as the body that decided to execute the imperial family. The story connects to the site through Nicholas II and Yevgeny Botkin, the doctor killed with the family.
people.goloschekin: Ural military commissar involved in deciding the Romanovs’ fate in summer 1918. The channel describes his journey to Moscow and discussions with Sverdlov. The material does not establish a direct written order from Moscow; conjecture about such an order should not be presented as a discovered document.
people.sverdlov: Chairman of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee in 1918. He appears in the Ipatiev House article in connection with discussions of the Romanovs’ fate and the later approval of the Ural Soviet’s decision. The article distinguishes these circumstances from the question of a direct written order from Moscow, which has not been found.
people.tretyakov: Commander of the 5th East Siberian Rifle Regiment, which defended the Jinzhou position in May 1904. The article on General Fok describes the dispute over unused reserves and the abandonment of the position. Tretyakov continued to challenge Fok publicly after the war.
people.grigorovich: Admiral and commander of the port of Port Arthur. At the surrender trial, he recalled that Fok’s appointment to command the land defences led the garrison to expect imminent capitulation. This participant’s testimony appears in the article on Fok’s disputed reputation.

geo.blagoveshchensk: City on the Amur opposite the Chinese bank. Qing troops shelled it during the Boxer Rebellion in 1900. In response, Russian authorities drove Chinese residents into the river; thousands died. The episode shows that the conflict reached beyond Beijing and Manchuria into Russia’s borderlands.
geo.chemulpo: Korean port, now Incheon. On 27 January (9 February) 1904, the cruiser Varyag and gunboat Koreets fought a Japanese squadron here. Back in port, Varyag was scuttled and Koreets blown up. The battle occurred on the same day as the first clash of the main forces off Port Arthur.
geo.dalnii: Russian commercial city and port built by the Chinese Eastern Railway Company from the late nineteenth century on Dalian Bay. It became Dairen under Japanese rule and is now Dalian. It should be distinguished from Port Arthur: the two cities developed for different purposes on different bays.
geo.golubinaya-buhta: Bay west of Port Arthur considered suitable for a Japanese landing in 1904. Concern for this sector explains its appearance on a satirical postcard that spring. The hindsight article compares the postcard with the defenders’ expectations before the siege had run its course.
geo.harbin: City and railway junction in Manchuria that grew during construction of the Chinese Eastern Railway. Harbin was besieged during the Boxer Rebellion in 1900, and the railway attacked. Its history connects with Dalny through the transport system linking inland Manchuria with the sea.
geo.koreya: The Korean peninsula was a principal focus of Russian-Japanese rivalry before the war. The channel examines diplomatic interests, the Yalu concession and the opening of hostilities. It supplies the regional setting of a conflict extending far beyond Port Arthur.
geo.kvantun: Historical name for the southern part of the Liaodong peninsula leased by Russia in 1898, including Port Arthur and Dalny. The lease rights passed to Japan after the war. Kwantung should not be confused with Guangdong province in southern China.
geo.kvzhd: The Chinese Eastern Railway linked Russia’s railway network through Manchuria. Its southern branch reached Kwantung, and the railway company built Dalny. The channel considers it as a transport project, financial enterprise and subject of international politics.
geo.lyaodun: Peninsula in northeastern China, with Dalian and Lüshun near its southern tip. Its geography shaped the ports and the land approaches to Port Arthur. Kotwicz and Borodovsky’s 1898 booklet describes it before construction of Russian Dalny began.
geo.lyaoyan: Manchurian city near which a major Russian-Japanese battle took place in 1904. Surrounding sorghum fields obstructed observation and concealed troop movements; plants had to be cut down in front of positions. Liaoyang’s story shows how unfamiliar terrain changed established ways of fighting.
geo.manchzhuriya: Historical region in northeastern China. The Chinese Eastern Railway, Russia’s military presence and rivalry with Japan made it a principal arena of the conflict. The channel discusses both actual events and plans for the region’s future, including the unrealised “Yellow Russia”.
geo.mukden: Historical name of Shenyang. A major battle between the Russian and Japanese armies took place around Mukden in 1905. The site considers it through war overviews, studies of everyday military life and memoirs. This was the Manchurian front, rather than part of the Port Arthur fortress.
geo.otsu: Japanese city where the policeman Tsuda Sanzō attacked the Russian heir Nicholas in 1891. The channel examines the attack, the Japanese court’s response and the end of the journey. The episode preceded the war by more than a decade.
geo.pekin: Capital of the Qing empire. The channel connects Beijing with the Boxer Rebellion, the siege of the Legation Quarter and the advance of the Eight-Nation Alliance in 1900. Russian units for the operation were drawn in part from Kwantung.
geo.port-artur: Historical European name for Lüshun; the Japanese reading is Ryojun. A Russian naval base and fortress stood here in 1898–1905. Lüshun is now part of Dalian, but historical Port Arthur and the commercial city of Dalny were separate towns.
geo.portsmut: American city whose name is associated with the 1905 peace treaty between Russia and Japan. President Theodore Roosevelt mediated the negotiations. The channel examines the financial exhaustion of both sides, Witte’s actions and the transfer of lease rights to Kwantung.
geo.sahalin: Island in the Russian Far East whose southern half passed to Japan under the Treaty of Portsmouth. The articles on Witte discuss this concession alongside Japan’s abandonment of an indemnity and the negotiator’s subsequent reputation, including his nickname “Count Half-Sakhalin”.
geo.shahe: Manchurian river that gave its name to the battle of October 1904. Shahe fighting and Putilov Hill occupy a central place in the commander-in-chief’s headquarters photographic album. Alongside battle pictures are dugouts, prisoners and the field army’s everyday life.
geo.shanhaiguan: Coastal pass and fortress at the eastern end of the Great Wall. It is the pass in Guandong, “east of the pass”, rendered in Russian as Kwantung. Originally, the Chinese term covered a much larger area than the southern Liaodong territory leased by Russia.
geo.sopka-putilovskaya: Height near the Shahe, taken by Russian troops in October 1904 and named after Major General Putilov. A series in the 1905 album shows it from the Japanese side, prisoners, captured guns, the general’s dugout and even a shell bursting on the hill. These are Manchurian army positions, rather than a Port Arthur fort.
geo.tsusima: Strait between Japan and the Korean peninsula, associated with the Battle of Tsushima in 1905. The defeat of the squadron arriving from the Baltic was the last major event of the naval war. In the channel’s overviews, it leads into the peace negotiations.
geo.tszinchzhou: Town and isthmus on the land approach to Kwantung. In May 1904, the position blocking the Japanese advance towards Dalny and Port Arthur was abandoned. The channel examines the battle through Tretyakov’s regiment, Fok’s reserves and naval support.
geo.uglovaya-gora: One of the heights on Port Arthur’s approaches. Kondratenko sought stronger garrisons here and on neighbouring Dagushan to hold the forward positions and buy time for the fortress. Heavy fighting later engulfed the area; the hill’s location should be checked against a historical plan.
geo.ulsan: Area off the Korean coast where the Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment fought Kamimura’s ships in 1904. Rurik sank, while Rossiya and Gromoboi returned damaged. The site discusses the battle in the detachment’s history and the review of Cruisers.
geo.vafangou: Area of a land battle in 1904, associated with modern Wafangdian. Here Yevgeny Botkin treated wounded men under shrapnel, carried them and gave them his horse. His Light and Shadows of the Russo-Japanese War shows the battle through medical care as well as staff decisions.
geo.vladivostok: Russian Pacific port and base of a separate cruiser detachment during the war. Its ships attacked Japanese sea communications. Vladivostok also appears in Dalny’s story through Vladimir Sakharov, an engineer who had previously worked on its commercial port.
geo.volchi-gory: Heights on Port Arthur’s approaches, where Russian troops suffered a setback in July 1904 before retreating to the fortress. Afterwards Kondratenko issued an order explaining the enemy’s superiority in men and artillery, and reminding soldiers that defence behind forts and concrete casemates would be different.
geo.yalu: River forming the border between China and Korea. The channel connects it with the timber concession, Bezobrazov’s circle and military operations in 1904. Commercial interests, diplomatic rivalry and the opening land campaign meet at this geographical junction.
geo.zheltoe-more: Sea bordering China and the Korean peninsula. Particularly important to Port Arthur’s history is the battle of 28 July (10 August) 1904, in which squadron commander Wilhelm Vitgeft was killed. The main Russian force returned to Port Arthur afterwards.
geo.moskva: Moscow’s Khodynka Field was the scene of a disaster during Nicholas II’s coronation celebrations in 1896. The channel examines the event’s organisation, Gilyarovsky’s testimony and the court’s response. Li Hongzhang was in Moscow at the same time, negotiating a Russian-Chinese alliance.
geo.ekaterinburg: City where Nicholas II, his family and their companions were killed in the Ipatiev House in 1918. Among them was Yevgeny Botkin, a doctor and author of memoirs of the Russo-Japanese War. The site explores this connection in its account of the family and the doctor.
geo.nikko: Japanese city whose temples Vasily Vereshchagin painted during his autumn 1903 visit. These works preceded his final journey: in spring 1904 he went to Port Arthur and died aboard Petropavlovsk. The artist’s article places peaceful Nikkō views beside his reflections on war.
geo.transsib: The Trans-Siberian Railway linked European Russia with the Far East. The Chinese Eastern Railway through Manchuria formed part of the development of this connection. For Port Arthur and Dalny, the railway meant access to the empire’s interior and a means of supply.
geo.iokogama: Japanese port where part of Boris Akunin’s The Diamond Chariot takes place. The channel’s review connects Yokohama in 1878 with Fandorin’s early experiences of Japan. This is a fictional setting; the novel’s events are not a documentary history of the city.
geo.svistov: Bulgarian town on the Danube, also called Sistova in Russian sources. Alexander Fok first won military distinction here in the war of 1877; his later life and burial are connected with the same area. On the channel, Svishtov links the beginning and end of the general’s life.

pre1898.card: Lüshunkou, the Beiyang Fleet’s base, the Sino-Japanese War and the Triple Intervention.
pre1898.lead: The Chinese harbour of Lüshunkou and Dalian Bay before the Russian lease: Li Hongzhang’s fleet, the war of 1894–1895 and the diplomacy that brought Russia to Liaodong.
intro: The harbour at Liaodong’s southern tip had a Chinese name long before Europeans arrived. Tradition says a Ming commander named it Lüshunkou, “bay of smooth sailing”, in 1371. The English name Port Arthur appeared during the Second Opium War, given by John Ward, captain of HMS Actaeon, in August 1860. The Russians later retained it.

In the 1880s Li Hongzhang, governor of the capital province of Zhili for almost a quarter-century, was building the Beiyang Fleet, with Lüshunkou as its base. Coastal batteries stood on Golden Hill under the Qing; the Russians later rebuilt them. An 1898 booklet describes Port Arthur in the 1870s as a village of 60–80 houses, and Dalianwan as ruined forts and one pier.

During the Sino-Japanese War of 1894–1895, Japan took the fortress in one day. Shimonoseki awarded Liaodong to Japan, but six days later Russia, Germany and France demanded its return: the Triple Intervention. Three years later Russia leased the peninsula itself.

The lease was preceded by the Franco-Russian alliance, the establishment of the Russo-Chinese Bank with French capital, the Moscow treaty of 1896 and the Chinese Eastern Railway concession. Tsarevich Nicholas’s Eastern journey and the Ōtsu attack also belong to this period.
pre1898.imageAlt: Li Hongzhang seated beside a column, wearing a robe and an order’s star
pre1898.caption: Li Hongzhang built the Beiyang Fleet, based at Lüshunkou.

dates.text: According to tradition, a Ming commander names the harbour Lüshunkou, “bay of smooth sailing”.
John Ward, captain of HMS Actaeon, gives the harbour the English name Port Arthur.
Lüshunkou becomes the base of Li Hongzhang’s Beiyang Fleet.
At Ōtsu, Japanese policeman Tsuda Sanzō wounds Tsarevich Nicholas with a sabre.
Sino-Japanese War: Japan captures Lüshunkou fortress in one day.
Treaty of Shimonoseki: China cedes Liaodong to Japan and pays 200 million taels.
Triple Intervention: Russia, Germany and France demand Liaodong’s return to China.
French capital establishes the Russo-Chinese Bank, later financier of the Chinese Eastern Railway.
Li Hongzhang signs an alliance with Russia in Moscow and agrees to construction of the Chinese Eastern Railway.
Korea’s King Gojong flees to the Russian legation in Seoul and rules from there for about a year.

russian.card: The Kwantung lease, a city built from scratch in four years, a fortress and a siege.
russian.lead: Seven years under the Russian flag: leasing Kwantung, building Dalny, the Pacific Squadron’s base and the siege of Port Arthur in 1904.
intro: On 15 (27) March 1898, Russia leased southern Liaodong for twenty-five years: Kwantung, an area of around 3,200 sq km. The navy needed Port Arthur because Vladivostok froze in winter. In 1899, nearby Dalny was founded as a commercial port and railway terminus.

The Chinese Eastern Railway Company built Dalny under Witte. Engineer Vladimir Sakharov designed the port and became city governor. Architect Kazimierz Skolimowski planned the city around circular Nikolayevskaya Square and ten radiating avenues. Within three years of its foundation, Dalny ranked second in China for port cargo. In summer 1903 Port Arthur became the capital of Admiral Alekseyev’s Far Eastern viceroyalty.

The war began during the night of 27 January (9 February) 1904, with Japanese destroyers attacking the squadron off Port Arthur. The fortress’s land defence lasted 221 days. General Kondratenko died on 2 (15) December 1904; surrender followed on 20 December 1904 (2 January 1905). Some 23,000–25,000 became prisoners, almost half Russia’s prisoners in that war.
The two cities spent less than seven years under the Russian flag; the Kwantung project cost the treasury at least 110 million rubles.
russian.imageAlt: Panorama of Port Arthur harbour: the Old Town, Golden Hill and the basins
russian.caption: Port Arthur harbour from Quail Hill. Smoke from an explosion below Golden Hill, probably during the 1904 bombardment.

dates.text: Russia leases Kwantung, including Port Arthur and Dalianwan, for twenty-five years.
Grand Duke Kirill Vladimirovich raises the Russian flag on Golden Hill.
Dalny is founded as a commercial port and Chinese Eastern Railway terminus.
Boxer Rebellion; by October the Russian army occupies all Manchuria.
Port Arthur becomes the capital of the Far Eastern viceroyalty.
Japan severs diplomatic relations with Russia.
Japanese destroyers attack the squadron on Port Arthur’s outer roadstead. The war begins.
Admiral Makarov, over 600 crew and painter Vereshchagin die aboard Petropavlovsk.
Battle of the Yellow Sea: the squadron fails to reach Vladivostok.
Japan takes 203 Metre Hill and begins shelling ships in the harbour.
General R. I. Kondratenko is killed at Fort No. II.
Port Arthur fortress surrenders to Japan.

russian.introTitle: A port, a city and a fortress in seven years

japanese.card: The Kwantung Leased Territory, South Manchuria Railway, Ōhiroba Square and the 1937 station.
japanese.lead: Forty years of Japanese rule: Dalny became Dairen, Port Arthur became Ryojun, and banks and railway offices filled out the Russian city plan.
intro: Under the Treaty of Portsmouth, 23 August (5 September) 1905, Japan acquired the Kwantung lease and the railway’s southern branch. Dalny became Dairen; Port Arthur, Ryojun. The Japanese read Kwantung’s characters as Kantō-shū, hence the Kwantung Army, formed from the territory’s garrison in 1919. The Twenty-One Demands extended the lease to 99 years in 1915.

The Japanese kept Dairen’s Russian plan and built around it. Nikolayevskaya Square, laid out but not developed by the Russians, became Ōhiroba. Between 1908 and 1936, police headquarters, a post office, city hall, banks and the South Manchuria Railway’s Yamato Hotel rose around the circle. Eight pre-war buildings survive. A new Dairen station opened in 1937.

Ryojun remained a military and administrative town. Japanese authorities landscaped the Russian military cemetery as a memorial to the fortress’s defenders. The Kwantung Government-General’s museum, now Lüshun Museum, opened in 1917. Japanese rule ended in August 1945 when Soviet troops entered both cities.
The map includes places from the Japanese period: the buildings around Ōhiroba Square, the station, the museum and the cherry garden at Longwangtang Reservoir.
japanese.imageAlt: Ōhiroba Square in Dairen from above: flowerbeds around the circle and a domed building in the centre
japanese.caption: Ōhiroba Square, formerly Nikolayevskaya, Dairen, c. 1940.

dates.text: Units of Japan’s Third Army enter Port Arthur.
Treaty of Portsmouth: Kwantung and the railway’s southern branch pass to Japan.
The South Manchuria Railway is established.
Police headquarters are built on Ōhiroba Square, Dairen.
The railway’s Yamato Hotel opens on Ōhiroba’s south side.
The Twenty-One Demands extend the Kwantung lease to 99 years.
The Kwantung Government-General’s museum opens in Ryojun, now Lüshun Museum.
The Kwantung Army is formed from the Japanese garrison; Dairen’s city hall is built.
Dairen’s new railway station opens.
The USSR enters the war against Japan.

japanese.introTitle: Dairen and Ryojun under Japanese administration

soviet.card: A naval base, joint administration and transfer to China.
soviet.lead: Ten years of a joint Soviet-Chinese base, from the landings of August 1945 to the withdrawal in 1955.
intro: The USSR entered the war against Japan on 9 August 1945. Under the Soviet-Chinese agreement of 1945, Port Arthur became a jointly used naval base and Dalny a free port. Soviet airborne detachments landed in both cities on 22 August.

On 2 September 1945, Japan’s surrender day, Stalin called the defeat of 1904 a “black stain” the older generation had waited forty years to erase. The Soviet canon of Port Arthur’s defence took shape at the same time. In 1946 Alexander Stepanov’s Port Arthur received the Stalin Prize: Kondratenko is the hero, Stessel responsible for surrender. Pikul’s books and the Lives of Remarkable People biography of Kondratenko continued this tradition.

After the People’s Republic was founded, Dalny passed to China in 1950; that year the two cities merged as Lüda. Soviet troops transferred Port Arthur’s museum to China on 1 February 1951. The troops left in 1955 and the base passed to the People’s Republic.

From 1945, Soviet servicemen who died locally were buried in Port Arthur’s Russian military cemetery, followed by Korean War casualties. A 1955 Soviet military monument stands at its entrance. According to differing sources, construction of the Sino-Soviet Friendship Tower in the New Town began in 1955.

dates.text: The USSR enters the war against Japan.
Soviet-Chinese agreement on joint use of Port Arthur as a naval base and Dalny as a free port.
Soviet airborne detachments land in Port Arthur and Dalny.
Japan surrenders. Stalin calls the defeat of 1904 a “black stain”.
A. Stepanov’s Port Arthur receives the Stalin Prize, First Class.
The People’s Republic of China is proclaimed.
Dalny passes to China; Port Arthur and Dalny merge as Lüda.
Soviet troops transfer Port Arthur’s museum to China.
A Soviet military monument is erected at the Russian military cemetery’s entrance.
Soviet troops withdraw; the Port Arthur base passes to the People’s Republic of China.

soviet.introTitle: A joint base and the return to China

modern.card: What survived, what was demolished and where to find traces of the old city.
modern.lead: Lüshun and Dalian after 1955: surviving buildings and fortifications, and a changing city. The remembrance of war and the study of the past form a separate theme.
intro: From 1955 Port Arthur was Chinese Lüshun. It belonged with Dalian to Lüda, renamed Dalian in 1981. Both former cities now form parts of Dalian, with almost seven million inhabitants.

Much survives: in Dalian, the circle of Nikolayevskaya, now Zhongshan Square, with eight pre-war buildings, the 1937 station and Yamato Hotel; in Lüshun, the land-front forts and intermediate works, Russian military cemetery and Lüshun Museum. Part of Lüshun remains an active naval base; the harbour is viewed from Quail Hill. The British consulate on the square was demolished in 1995.

The remembrance of earlier periods is a theme of its own: the military cemetery, museums, monuments and fortifications that can be visited today. This section also brings together material on how this heritage is preserved and studied.
modern.imageAlt: A 10-inch coastal gun at Fortification No. 5 in Lüshun
modern.caption: A coastal gun at Fortification No. 5 in Lüshun. Its authenticity has not been established. Photograph by the channel’s author.

dates.text: Port Arthur becomes Chinese Lüshun within the city of Lüda.
Lüda is renamed Dalian.
The British consulate on Zhongshan Square is demolished.
Russian specialists restore Lüshun’s Russian military cemetery.
Japanese archives publish an online war-centenary exhibition.
The Russian Orthodox Church canonises Yevgeny Botkin, doctor and author of Light and Shadows of the Russo-Japanese War.

modern.introTitle: The city after 1955 and the memory of its past

zodchiy-plan-dalnego-1904.title: Two words beneath a plan: Nikolayevskaya Square
zodchiy-plan-dalnego-1904.intro: An old name, a circle and radiating streets: a few details on this plan offer a way into today’s Zhongshan Square.
zodchiy-plan-dalnego-1904.caption: Plan of Nikolayevskaya Square, reproduced in the channel post.
zodchiy-plan-dalnego-1904.transcriptionNote: Only the clear caption is transcribed. Small annotations and the central outline have not been decoded. Attribution to the paper follows the channel post; the original page is not yet checked. A plan records a proposal, not completed construction.

sections.title: Start with the name
paragraphs: “Николаевская площадь” translates as “Nikolayevskaya Square”; its Chinese equivalent is 尼古拉广场. The drawing preserves the Russian name of the place now known as 中山广场, Zhongshan Square. The old caption is a first clue to a familiar urban space.

sections.title: A circle and ten directions
paragraphs: The square has a recognisable framework: a circle with streets radiating outwards. The museum describes a diameter of 213 metres and ten roads. Follow the streets towards the ring, and notice the planting groups between them. The drawing invites you to look beyond an individual building to the connections across the city.

sections.title: The plan and the city that followed
paragraphs: The Chinese museum account distinguishes the Russian layout from Japanese-period construction. The familiar circle and the façades around it belong to different stages.

Yamato Hotel offers a comparison: the government heritage entry dates its construction to 1909–1914. At Zhongshan Square today, look from one façade to the whole circle; on the old plan, follow that circle into the radiating streets. The sources offer two ways of reading the same place.
